Possible symptom of leprosy to be examined by the priest
H0934.detail:
1. A visible white or pale spot on a person's skin — something that stands out and causes concern. In Leviticus 13:2, it speaks of a "tumor, scab, or white spot resembling a leprous sore." 
2. A persistent mark after a wound or burn that has healed. In Leviticus 13:23, the spot "remaining in the same place" is declared a "scar of the ulcer." 
3. A sign of a serious skin disease (leprosy) that only the priest can identify by examining it closely. In Leviticus 13:25, if the hair turns white in the spot and it appears deep, it is a diagnosis of leprosy.
H0934.origine: Hebrew word designating what is white, bright, or clear — a visible mark of pale color on the skin. The root evokes the luminous or whitish aspect of these skin manifestations.
H0934.emploi: This word appears 11 times, all usages in Leviticus 13-14, at the heart of the purity code concerning skin diseases. It always designates a visible spot that a man or woman must show to the priest. The word does not change meaning: it remains clinical and descriptive. What the priest must distinguish is whether the spot indicates true leprosy (by its depth, hair color, its evolution) or a simple harmless scar.
H0934.portee: This term reminds us that the Mosaic law did not speak of abstract diseases, but of real, visible cases that required judgment and compassion. The role of the priest was not to punish, but to examine, discern, and pronounce purity or impurity — anticipating the healing and restoration of the sick person within the community of Israel.

sens: to move toward a place, arrive at a destination
to enter a closed or defined space
to present oneself before someone
to occur, happen, come to someone
to lead someone, bring in
to reach a state or moment
H0935G.detail:
1. To move toward a place, arrive at a destination: the verb expresses the movement of a person or thing approaching or going to a place. Example: "Balaam refused to come with us" (Numbers 22:14). 
2. To enter a closed or defined space: the idea of crossing a threshold, penetrating a place. Example: "You shall enter the ark, you and your sons" (Genesis 6:18). 
3. To present oneself before someone: to come into their presence, to appear, to show oneself to someone intentionally. Example: "The sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord" (Job 2:1). 
4. To occur, happen, come to someone: denotes an event, a situation that manifests, often without the subject's control. Example: "When you advance to fight the Chaldeans" (Jeremiah 33:5), the action occurs as a reality that arrives. 
5. To lead someone, bring in: in a causative sense, it is the action of bringing or leading someone or something to or into a place. 
6. To reach a state or moment: to arrive at being or finding oneself in a certain condition, to accomplish a given state.
H0935G.origine: The verb בּוֹא (bo) comes from an ancient Semitic root expressing the movement of approach and penetration. The basic image is that of a person moving and crossing a boundary (a threshold, an entrance, a distance). Verbs of the same family exist in Arabic (ba'a) and Aramaic. In biblical Hebrew, the two main forms are the simple form (Qal), which describes the action in an active sense ("to come," "to enter"), and the causative form (Hiphil), which means "to bring in," "to lead," "to introduce."
H0935G.emploi: With 1,753 occurrences, בּוֹא is one of the most frequent verbs in the Old Testament. It appears in nearly all books, from the narratives of Genesis to the oracles of the prophets. Its usages cover both the concrete sense (someone physically moving) and the figurative sense (an event occurring, a moment arriving). In Genesis, it describes the movements of the patriarchs and the entry into the ark (Genesis 6:18, 7:7). In the historical books (Samuel, Kings), it expresses the movement of kings, messengers, and armies. The verb can also mean "to return" or "to come back" (Numbers 22:14). Its meaning nuances according to the context: simple spatial movement, act of entering, appearing before God, or occurrence of an event.
H0935G.portee: For the biblical reader, this verb evokes the mystery of movement and divine providence: humans "come" to places and people, but also events "come" to us according to God's plan. Understanding this word helps grasp how the Bible describes not only our voluntary actions but also what happens to us, as if the world enters us through paths we do not always control. It is an invitation to discern, in every arrival or occurrence, the hand of the One who governs.

sens: The region through which one enters the territory of Hamath, north of Israel
The geographical point marking the northern border of the promised lands to Israel
A passage or boundary between two territories
H0935H.detail:
1. The "entrance of Hamath" designates the passage or access point to the region of Hamath, this fertile area in the north (present-day Syria). The word "entrance" translates the Hebrew idea of passing, crossing a threshold: it is the point from which one ascends to Hamath. In Numbers 13:21, the spies ascend to the "entrance" of Hamath during their exploration of the land. 
2. This expression primarily marks a border, the northern limit of the territory that Israel must conquer or controls. In Joshua 13:5, it is to the "entrance" of Hamath that the promised lands extend; in 1 Chronicles 13:5, David gathers Israel from Egypt to this same boundary point. It is a major political and territorial landmark. 
3. The word can also designate a passage or way: in Numbers 34:8, it is said that the border must "pass" through Hamath, and in Ezekiel 47:20, it speaks of the side that extends "opposite" Hamath, indicating a direction or line.
H0935H.origine: The Hebrew word לְבוֹא (bo) literally means "to enter" or "to go into." Combined with חֲמָת (Hamath), it forms a unique geographical term: "the entrance of Hamath." This compound becomes a proper place name, fixed, always designating the same well-known border crossing for the ancient Israelites.
H0935H.emploi: This expression appears about six times in the Hebrew Bible, always to delineate the borders of Israel's territory. It appears in Numbers (the exploration and limits of the conquered land), in Joshua (the inheritance of the territory), in Judges (the neighboring nations), in 1 Chronicles (the extent of David's kingdom), and in Ezekiel (the vision of the future borders of restored Israel). It serves as a constant geographical marker, the quintessential northern limit of the lands of Israel.
H0935H.portee: For the believer, the "entrance of Hamath" reminds us that God sets defined boundaries for His people. It symbolizes the exact extent of the promise made: no more, no less than what was intended. This northern limit also emphasizes that the promised land had a concrete geographical reality, not an abstract one.

sens: Cross a threshold, pass through a door or a limit to arrive inside a place
Head towards a location, approach, arrive at a destination
Go, move in a direction
Penetrate, introduce oneself (in a literal or figurative sense)
Arrive at a moment or a state
Reach, attain to
H0935I.detail:
1. Cross a threshold or entrance: the word describes the action of passing through a door, a limit, or a boundary to arrive inside a space. In 1 Kings 18:46, Elijah "runs before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel" — he goes to the access point of the city. This is the concrete movement of someone who enters somewhere.
2. Head towards a location, approach: the verb also marks the act of setting out towards a destination, gradually getting closer. In Joshua 8:11, the warriors "approached" (literally "arrived") in front of the city; in 1 Samuel 20:19, David goes down "to the" bottom of the place — it conveys the idea of converging towards a point.
3. Go, move in a direction: this is a more general movement, without emphasis on arriving at the goal. In Genesis 25:18, it is said that the sons of Ishmael lived "while going towards Assyria" — the movement itself.
4. Extend to (with the spatial sense of limit): when the verb marks an extent, it expresses that something goes, extends "to" a point. In Genesis 10:19, the boundaries of the Canaanites go "towards" Gerar — it conveys the idea of direction and limit reached.
5. Arrive at a moment or come to pass: the verb can also mean that an event "occurs", "happens". This is a more abstract usage where the movement becomes temporal.
6. Reach, attain to: in certain contexts, the verb expresses the idea of success in reaching a state or a number, such as "being counted" or listed among.
H0935I.origine: The verb בּוֹא (bo) comes from a primitive root that fundamentally means "to move towards", "to go in a direction". The basic image is that of bodily movement: someone physically moving from one point to another. This is why the verb can mean both "enter" (the movement crossing a limit), "come" (the movement towards someone), "go" (the movement in general), and "reach" (the movement resulting in an outcome). It is one of the most frequent movement verbs in biblical Hebrew.
H0935I.emploi: The verb בּוֹא appears 22 times in the provided usages, primarily in the historical books (Genesis, Joshua, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles). In the simple form (Qal), it means "to enter", "to come", "to go" or "to arrive": the soldiers "arrive" in front of Ai (Joshua 8:11), David goes down "to" a place (1 Samuel 20:19). In the causative form (Hiphil), it becomes "to bring", "to introduce", "to lead": one "brings" someone into a place. The verb is also used to express geographical limits, as in Genesis 10:19 where it marks territorial extent ("towards", "until"). In all these contexts, it is the movement — whether physical, spatial, or even temporal — that remains the central idea.
H0935I.portee: This simple verb reminds the reader that biblical life is marked by movement: going, coming, entering, progressing. It is a key word for understanding how God calls His people to move, to advance, to cross thresholds. When Israel "enters" the Promised Land or when a prophet "comes" to a king, this movement expresses obedience or God's purpose. The verb also invites reflection on our own spiritual movements — where are we going, to whom are we turning, what limits are we crossing in our walk of faith?

sens: To have many years, to be very old
To progress towards the end of life
To approach the natural end of existence
H0935J.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the state of a person who has lived a long time and whose body bears the marks of age. Abraham and Sarah in Genesis 18:11 are "advanced in age": their bodies are worn, their strength diminished, as indicated by the context which recalls that Sarah "could no longer hope to have children". It is an observable, concrete physical state. 2. By extension, the word evokes the idea of progression in the time of life, as if one is advancing towards the outcome of their existence. Joshua in Joshua 13:1 and 23:1-2 is "advanced in age": he has fulfilled his mission, the time to retire is approaching. 3. The word also emphasizes the wisdom and experience accumulated: those who are advanced in age have traversed many years and possess moral authority. Jesse in 1 Samuel 17:12 is described this way, the father of David, a figure of seniority and stability.
H0935J.origine: The Hebrew word בּוֹא (bo) primarily means "to enter" or "to come". The expression "advanced in age" uses a form of this verb to express the idea of "progression" or "advancement" in the time of life. It is an image: life is a path where one "enters" and "progresses", and the one who is "advanced" has traveled a long way. The same root produces in Hebrew derivatives related to movement and entry into a space or situation.
H0935J.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the provided usages, always in the expression "advanced in age" to qualify patriarchs and leaders of Israel: Abraham (Genesis 18:11 and 24:1), Joshua (Joshua 13:1, 23:1-2), Jesse (1 Samuel 17:12), and King David (1 Kings 1:1, although not detailed). It marks a narrative turning point: these men have accomplished the tasks that God entrusted to them and are approaching the end of their lives. The context always emphasizes the fulfillment of a mission before this advancement in age. It is a word that reveres seniority and acknowledges human limits in the face of time.
H0935J.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that life on earth is limited and inevitably progresses towards its end. It invites recognition of a form of authority and wisdom in the elderly. But above all, it shows that God entrusts His greatest works to aged men, like Abraham, Joshua, and David: this reveals that true strength is not physical youth, but trust in God and the fulfillment of His will. Aging while accomplishing the mission that God has given becomes a blessing.

sens: The moment when the sun disappears below the horizon at the end of the day
The action of lying down, of reclining to sleep or rest
To enter, to penetrate into a place
To happen, to occur, to take place
H0935K.detail:
1. The setting of the sun is the precise moment when the celestial body of the day disappears on the horizon. It is a natural marker of time that structures the day. The Bible often uses this moment to mark important events: Joshua asks God to stop the sun so that it does not have time to set during the battle (Joshua 10:13), and at the time of the new creation, Isaiah prophesies that there will be no more setting of the sun because God Himself will be the eternal light (Isaiah 60:20).

2. The setting refers to the action of lying down: Jacob lies down in a place to sleep and receives his vision of angels there (Genesis 28:11). The Law protects the poor worker by requiring that his garment be returned to him at sunset, so that he does not sleep naked (Deuteronomy 24:13).

3. To enter or penetrate into a place is the broadest sense of the Hebrew word from which this translation comes. The original verb expresses the movement of crossing a threshold, moving from one place to another.

4. To happen or occur: events "happen" or "take place," like the vengeance that "is fulfilled" on enemies (Joshua 10:13).
H0935K.origine: The Hebrew word bo fundamentally means "to enter" or "to go in." It is a very common verb in biblical Hebrew. The sense of "setting" (of the sun) naturally derives from this: the sun "enters" below the horizon. The same verb is used for all movements of entry or arrival: to enter a house, to arrive at a place, to happen. This image of movement inward or crossing a boundary is at the heart of the word.
H0935K.emploi: The verb bo appears hundreds of times in the Old Testament with very varied meanings. In the provided usages, it is systematically translated as "setting" (of the sun or moon) — a pivotal moment of the day that the Bible uses to date events, set legal deadlines, or mark blessings. The setting of the sun also delineates times of work and rest according to the Law. It is a concrete and universal marker, recognizable to all, that God Himself created to measure time.
H0935K.portee: The setting of the sun reminds us that time flows under the governance of God. It is a moment of transition: the end of work, a call to rest, a limit to deadlines. For the people of God, it is also a promise: Isaiah 60:20 promises a day when there will be no more setting of the sun, for God Himself will be the eternal light. What is constant and natural now will one day yield to the permanent presence of God.

sens: To penetrate into a place, a space
To come, to arrive somewhere
To consummate the marital act with a woman
To engage in a relationship, a covenant
To happen, to arrive as an event
H0935L.detail:
1. To penetrate into a place, a space: the word describes the concrete action of entering somewhere. In Judges 16:1, Samson "went in to her" (to the prostitute): it is crossing a threshold, penetrating inside.
2. To come, to arrive somewhere: a similar sense but emphasizing movement or arrival rather than the act of crossing a door. In 1 Samuel 1:19, after worship, they "returned" to Ramah: they went back home.
3. To consummate the marital act with a woman: a specific and modest use of the verb to designate the physical relationship between a man and a woman. It is "to enter" that means "to know" in the biblical sense. In 1 Samuel 1:19, "Elkanah knew Hannah" uses the same verb.
4. To engage in a relationship, a covenant through marriage: Joshua 23:12 warns Israel not to "unite" by marriage with the surrounding nations, which means entering into dangerous marital and familial relationships for the faith.
5. To happen, to arrive as an event: a figurative sense where the verb describes what happens or occurs, rather than a physical movement.
H0935L.origine: The verb "to enter" comes from the Hebrew root בוא (bo), one of the most common in biblical Hebrew. It fundamentally expresses the idea of movement toward a place, of passing from one space to another. The root has given rise to many derivatives. When in the Hiphil (causative form), it means "to bring in, to lead, to bring." It is a very simple and fundamental verb in the Hebrew language.
H0935L.emploi: The verb appears five times in the provided usages, with meanings that vary slightly according to context. In Judges 16:1, it is literally "to enter someone's house." In 1 Samuel 1:19, it is "to return" and also "to know" his wife (marital relationship). In Joshua 23:12 and 1 Kings 11:2, it concerns marriage and alliances with other peoples, which pose a spiritual danger for Israel. In 2 Samuel 17:25, Jithra "went to" Abigail, suggesting a marital relationship. The verb thus oscillates between the concrete sense of physical movement and the sense of intimate relationship.
H0935L.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of the importance of spiritual boundaries and choices of covenant. When the Bible warns against "entering" into relationships with those who do not share the faith, it protects the heart against influences that undermine faithfulness to God. The word also invites vigilance in human relationships that deeply engage us.

sens: To enter, to come into a place
To arrive, to occur, to take place
To realize, to bring to completion a word or a promise
To be enumerated, to be counted among
H0935M.detail:
1. To physically enter a place or to go there: the verb describes a concrete movement toward a place. This is the primary and most basic sense, which appears in narratives of movements and displacements.
2. To arrive or occur: the idea of an action that takes place or an event that happens. In 1 Samuel 9:6, "everything he says will surely come to pass" expresses the assurance that the prophet's words will inevitably be fulfilled.
3. To fulfill, to realize or to bring to completion: this is one of the most important nuances in a religious context. When God promises something, what "comes" or "is fulfilled" is the realization of that promise. In Joshua 23:15, "all the good words that the Lord had spoken to you have been fulfilled" shows that God's promises become reality. In 1 Samuel 10:7, "when these signs have come to you" refers to the effective realization of the promised signs.
4. To be enumerated or counted: the verb can mean to be included in a group or a list, to be taken into account among others.
H0935M.origine: The verb בּוֹא (bo) comes from a very ancient and general root that expresses movement toward a place or the coming of a reality. The family of the word includes nouns like "entry" or "coming." In biblical Hebrew, this verb is one of the most common: it primarily describes physical movement, then broadens its meaning to everything that "comes" or "arrives," including divine words and promises that "are fulfilled." This progression from the concrete to the spiritual reflects the Hebrew vision where the word acts: what God says comes into existence.
H0935M.emploi: This verb appears 10 times in the provided usages, mainly to express the fulfillment of God's word. In Genesis 6:13, "the end of all flesh has come before me" uses the verb to indicate that a judgment is determined and will come. In Joshua 23:15, the fulfillment of God's words ("have been fulfilled") shows how divine promises are realized. The context of missed promises is also present: in 1 Samuel 9:6, "everything he says will surely come to pass" expresses the reliability of the prophet. In 1 Chronicles 4:10, Jabez's prayer asks that God "grants what he has asked," showing how fulfillment relates to divine listening and grace. The verb thus covers the arrival of an event, the coming of a person, the realization of a promise or a threat, and the certainty that divine words are fulfilled.
H0935M.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of God's absolute reliability: when He speaks, what He says necessarily happens. God's promises do not remain void; they "come" and are "fulfilled." At the same time, God's threats and judgments also inevitably come to pass. It is a call to take the divine word seriously, to rely on it as a believer, and to recognize that history unfolds according to God's design.

sens: Arrive somewhere, enter a place
Present oneself, appear
Occur, happen
Attack, descend upon (an enemy)
Besiege a city, lay siege to it
H0935N.detail:
1. The basic meaning is to arrive or to enter: to move toward a place and enter it. It is the simple movement of a person going somewhere. For example, in the text of Deuteronomy, it speaks of coming to battle.

2. The word also means to show oneself, to appear: to be present, to manifest oneself before someone. In 2 Chronicles 32:1, Sennacherib "appeared": he suddenly showed up, arriving in a notable way.

3. To come can mean to occur, to take place: an event comes to pass, it happens. This is a broader meaning, applicable to anything that occurs.

4. The word describes the action of descending upon an enemy, attacking: coming against someone with hostile intent. It is coming with a warlike charge.

5. Finally, to besiege: to surround a city, to enter it to take it. In 2 Chronicles 32:1, Sennacherib "entered Judah and besieged the fortified cities." The verb "entered" here conveys the idea of coming against to besiege.
H0935N.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses movement, the transition from one point to another. It is a very ancient and common word in biblical Hebrew, which retains its fundamental sense of locomotion but enriches itself with nuances depending on the context: to enter, to arrive, to occur, to attack. The root evokes the action of setting out and reaching a destination.
H0935N.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament. It appears in several forms: the simple mode "come" (Qal), the causative form "to bring, to introduce" (Hiphil), and the passive form "to be brought" (Hophal). The provided usages show its flexibility: in Joshua 8:29, "to set" translates the verb applied to the sun setting (descending toward the horizon); in 2 Chronicles 32:1, "appeared" and "entered" render the same root in military contexts — the appearance of the enemy king and his invasion of the territory. The verb thus applies to the movement of people, celestial bodies, events, and the action of war. Its six biblical usages provided all concern the context of siege and the arrival of an army.
H0935N.portee: This verb reminds the reader that God controls comings and goings, arrivals and events: who comes, when, and with what power. It is a verb of action and movement that anchors biblical history in the concrete reality of movements and battles, showing that God acts in visible history. For the believer, it invites recognition of God's providence in the events that occur.

sens: Region in the north of Palestine, northern boundary of Israel
Entrance or access to the region of Hamath
Geographical landmark to delineate a territory
H0935O.detail: 1. Lebo Hamath refers to a region located in the north of Palestine, serving as a natural boundary of the territory of Israel. In 1 Kings 8:65 and 2 Chronicles 7:8, a large crowd gathered "from the vicinity of Hamath to the brook of Egypt" during the celebration of the feast, indicating that this was a well-known region. 2. The word "Lebo" literally means "entrance" or "access," which emphasizes that this region marked the entry or passage to the land of Hamath. In 2 Kings 14:25, it is written that King Jeroboam "restored the borders of Israel from the entrance of Hamath" — it was a recognized boundary point. 3. Lebo Hamath served as a landmark to define the borders of Israel and to describe the extent of the territory that God had promised or restored — Ezekiel 47:15 uses it to outline the boundaries of a vision of the restored land.
H0935O.origine: The name is formed from two elements: "Lebo" comes from the Hebrew verb meaning "to enter" or "to come," and "Hamath" is the name of the main city in this northern region. Together, "Lebo Hamath" literally means "the entrance of Hamath" or "the passage to Hamath," describing a strategically significant geographical point. It is an example of a geographical name that combines a verb and a place name to precisely locate a region.
H0935O.emploi: This term appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to mark a territorial boundary of Israel. In 1 Kings 8:65 and 2 Chronicles 7:8 (two parallel accounts), it designates the northern point to which the crowd had come to celebrate the feast under Solomon. In 2 Kings 14:25, it is the boundary that King Jeroboam had restored according to the promise of the prophet Jonah. In Ezekiel 47:15, the prophet uses it to describe the borders of the land in a vision of future restoration. Each time, it serves as a marker to indicate either the extent of a territory or the origin of people coming from that distant north.
H0935O.portee: Lebo Hamath reminds us that God's promise regarding the land of Israel had precise boundaries, from north to south. This name also emphasizes how God protected and restored the boundaries of His people's territory according to His word spoken through the prophets. For the Christian reader, it is a concrete proof of God's faithfulness in keeping His geographical promises just as He does for all His promises.

sens: To move from one place to another, to arrive somewhere
To bring, carry, or transport something from one place to another
To lead, bring someone somewhere
To cause the arrival or occurrence of something
To enter a place, to penetrate inside
H0935P.detail:
1. To move from one place to another, to arrive somewhere: this is the simple movement of a person going from one location to another. When Jacob arrives at Laban's, Laban "comes" to meet him (Genesis 29:13); it is the act of presenting oneself, of appearing.

2. To bring, carry, or transport something: this meaning concerns the action of moving a physical object from one point to another. Cain "brings" an offering (Genesis 4:3), Noah "brings" everything that can be eaten (Genesis 6:17), and money is "brought" to the house of the Lord (2 Kings 22:4).

3. To lead, bring someone somewhere: this is to guide a person to a destination. The Lord "brings" Israel back to the land of their fathers (Deuteronomy 30:5); similarly, one "brings" someone to a specific place.

4. To cause the arrival or occurrence of something: this meaning includes immaterial realities and events. The Lord brings "evils" upon Jerusalem (Jeremiah 44:2) and upon Israel (Nehemiah 13:18) — this is not a physical arrival, but the fulfillment or realization.

5. To enter a place, to penetrate inside: the action of crossing a threshold or moving from one enclosure to another, often related to the sanctuary or a building.
H0935P.origine: This verb comes from a primary Hebrew root expressing directional movement. The basic image is that of moving toward a given point — a person or thing moving in space to reach a destination. It is one of the most frequently used movement verbs in biblical Hebrew. The verbal forms allow for the expression of both simple action (Qal: to come, to go) and causative action (Hiphil: to cause to come, to bring, to carry), or the experience of undergoing this action (Hophal: to be brought, to be led).
H0935P.emploi: This verb is one of the most used in the Hebrew Bible, with over 526 occurrences. It appears in almost every book, from the Pentateuch to the Prophets, and denotes either physical movement (Genesis 2:19, where the animals "come" to man), the transport of objects (Leviticus 2:2, bringing an offering), or causation (causing an event to occur: Jeremiah 44:2, "to bring" calamity). The context always clarifies whether it is a simple arrival, a material offering, or a divine intervention that produces effects. It is also a basic verb for narrating the movements of characters in stories: Abraham goes, Jacob comes, the sons of Jacob bring gifts. Its use extends from historical narration to the theological language of judgment and blessing.
H0935P.portee: This verb reminds us that God governs the movements and events of the world. When He "brings" calamity or blessing, it affirms that nothing escapes His sovereignty. For the believer, recognizing the significance of this verb means seeing that even events that seem to be the result of chance or human malice remain under divine control. It also invites responsibility: we who "bring" our offerings or our deeds before God are seen and judged. It is a covenant verb: God "brings back" His people, "brings" blessing, as acts of love and faithfulness.

sens: To show disdain towards someone or something, to judge it as worthless
To regard as nothing, to treat without respect
To deliberately reject, to refuse to listen
H0936.detail:
1. To despise is to look down on someone or something as if it has no value. It is an attitude of the heart that manifests as disdain. In Proverbs 1:7, fools "despise" wisdom — they reject it, refusing to consider it precious. It is more than simple disapproval: it is a judgment of contempt.
2. Despising also involves treating someone with a lack of respect, humiliating them through our attitude. When one "despises" their neighbor (Proverbs 11:12), they regard them as unworthy of consideration. It is a sin because it violates the dignity that God has given to each person.
3. To despise is also to refuse to listen, to deliberately reject what is said to us. One who "despises" the word of God (Proverbs 13:13) does not take it seriously; they push it away. This attitude leads to destruction.
H0936.origine: The Hebrew verb בּוּז comes from a root that evokes the idea of rejecting, keeping at a distance. It is a word that expresses an attitude of the heart — not just a thought, but an active feeling of disdain. The word belongs to the realm of personal judgment and social contempt: it describes how one looks at someone, how one treats them.
H0936.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Proverbs (at least 6 occurrences). It serves as a warning: Proverbs constantly shows the consequences of contempt — one loses oneself when one despises (Proverbs 13:13), one commits a sin (Proverbs 14:21), one covers oneself with shame (Proverbs 23:22). The word denotes a dangerous attitude, contrary to wisdom. It opposes the fear of the Lord and respect: one who despises the word or their neighbor chooses the fool over the wise.
H0936.portee: To despise is a sin that reveals a heart far from the wisdom of God. It reminds us that our attitude towards others and towards the word of God has serious consequences: contempt destroys the one who harbors it and wounds the one who is its object. Learning to respect even those we disapprove of is a mark of Christian maturity and fear of the Lord.

sens: Feeling of disdain, devaluation towards someone or something
State of being belittled, humiliated, despised by others
Shame or dishonor attached to a person or situation
H0937.detail:
1. Contempt is primarily this feeling of rejection and devaluation that one experiences towards someone. It is to look down on someone, to judge them unworthy of respect. When Judah fears that his daughter-in-law Tamar will be discovered, he wants to avoid "contempt" — that is, being ridiculed, treated as unworthy of honor (Genesis 38:23).
2. Contempt is also what one suffers: it is being belittled, humiliated by others who judge you as worthless. Job sees this clearly: the unfortunate are destined for contempt, while the rich escape it (Job 12:5). God can pour contempt upon the mighty, reducing them to powerlessness and shame (Job 12:21).
3. Finally, it is the shame, the reproach that weighs upon someone or their honor. The psalmist fears the contempt of families, this collective judgment that would cover him with dishonor (Psalms 31:34; Psalms 123:3).
H0937.origine: The Hebrew word bûz evokes the idea of rejecting, pushing away. It is related to a root that literally means to set aside or disdain. Contempt arises from judgment: one pushes away something or someone they consider worthless, unworthy of honor or respect. It is a word that regularly appears in the wisdom and prayers of the Hebrew Bible to describe the wounds one bears — human or before God.
H0937.emploi: The word bûz appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Psalms, Job, and Proverbs — books that explore suffering, injustice, and wisdom. In historical narratives (like Genesis 38:23), it is the fear of being socially despised. In Job and the Psalms, contempt is an existential experience: suffered by the unfortunate and the oppressed, sometimes poured out by God upon the proud (Job 12:21; Psalms 107:40). The Psalms show a heart that cries under the weight of others' contempt (Psalms 123:3-4), while Proverbs notes that contempt arises from self-doubt (Proverbs 12:8).
H0937.portee: Contempt wounds deeply, and the psalmist teaches us to bring it before God in prayer rather than hide it. The Bible also reveals that God knows those who endure contempt, and that it is never a shame before Him. For the Christian who suffers judgment from others or the world, this word reminds us that only God's gaze truly matters.

sens: Son of Nahor and Milcah, great-nephew of Abraham
H0938G.detail: Buz is the second son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and Milcah. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:21, where he is listed among Nahor's children: "Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram." He is part of Abraham's patriarchal family, representing a younger branch of Nahor's descendants.
H0938G.origine: The name Buz means "contempt" or "disdain" in Hebrew, evoking a notion of rejection or belittlement. It has no apparent connection to the events or qualities of the mentioned character. It is a theophoric or symbolic name, like many in the patriarchal genealogies, which likely reflects realities of family or social life in ancient times.
H0938G.emploi: Buz is cited only once in the Scriptures, in Genesis 22:21, where the list of the twelve children Nahor had with Milcah after Isaac's birth is given. This genealogical passage situates Buz within Abraham's lineage and shows the familial ties of the peoples surrounding Israel. Although little known, Buz thus appears in the family structure that connects Abraham to his Mesopotamian cousins.

sens: man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
father of Jahdo
H0938H.detail: 1. Buz is a man belonging to the tribe of Gad, mentioned only once in the Bible during the enumeration of Gadite genealogies (1 Chronicles 5:14). 2. He is identified as the father of Jahdo, meaning he appears in a genealogical chain that traces back to Michael and Gilead.
H0938H.origine: The name Buz literally means "contempt" or "disdain" in Hebrew. It is a personal name that belonged to several characters in Israel's ancient history, notably a son of Nahor (Abraham's brother). Here, it designates a Gadite from the period of the divided monarchy.
H0938H.emploi: Buz appears only once in the biblical text (1 Chronicles 5:14), in the context of the genealogy of the children of Gad. This verse presents him as a link in a long genealogical chain: Michael, Jechishai, Jahdo (his son), Buz, Jaroach, Gilead, and Huri. This type of mention anchors the identity of the Gadites in the history and genealogy of Israel.

sens: Region or tribe of Arabia
H0938I.detail: Buz is a region or tribe of Arabian territory, mentioned alongside Dedan and Tema in Jeremiah's prophecy against the nations. These Arab peoples are targeted by divine judgment, particularly those who shave the corners of their beards, a practice related to their religious or cultural customs.
H0938I.origine: The name Buz literally means "contempt" or "disdain" in Hebrew, which could reflect a contemptuous attitude towards this region or its population; however, as a proper name designating a region or people, the meaning of the name is not directly relevant to its geographical identification. Buz appears in biblical texts as a well-known region of the ancient Arab world.
H0938I.emploi: Buz appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 25:23, in the context of a prophecy by Jeremiah listing the nations and peoples subject to divine judgment. It is classified among the Arab peoples alongside Dedan and Tema, and is characterized by the practice of shaving the corners of the beard, a distinct Arab custom. This unique mention places Buz in the prophetic geography of the ancient Middle East.

sens: feeling of disdain or devaluation towards someone or something
lack of respect or honor
insult or affront
H0939.detail:
1. Contempt is the feeling of one who considers someone or something as unworthy of esteem or honor. In Nehemiah 4:4, the enemies of Nehemiah and the Jewish people "despise" them, meaning they treat them as if they have no value or importance.
2. This feeling manifests through words or acts of disdain: insults, humiliations, refusal to recognize a person's dignity. In the cited passage, contempt is expressed through insults hurled against the builders of the wall of Jerusalem.
3. It is a personal offense, an affront to honor that justifies a reaction: Nehemiah asks God to avenge this contempt by bringing the insults back upon those who uttered them.
H0939.origine: The Hebrew word בּוּזָה (buzah) comes from the root בוז (buz), which fundamentally means "to despise" or "to regard as nothing." This root expresses the idea of rejecting something or someone as worthless. The word appears in contexts where a person's honor or dignity is denied or attacked.
H0939.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 4:4. It designates the contempt that the adversaries of the Jewish people express against the builders of the wall of Jerusalem. Nehemiah, faced with these insults and this disdain, intercedes with God for the contempt to be turned back against those who expressed it. This context shows that contempt is not merely an internal feeling but a public attack against the honor of God's people.
H0939.portee: Contempt is presented here as a form of spiritual and moral aggression. In the face of mockery and insults, Nehemiah does not retaliate with violence or insult: he appeals to God. This passage teaches the believer that when one suffers contempt or humiliation for the faith, one can entrust the matter to God and ask for justice, knowing that He is aware of our sufferings and our dignity.

sens: ancestor of Elihu, father or grandfather of Barakel
H0940.detail: 1. Buz is an ancestor of Elihu mentioned in the book of Job. Elihu introduces himself as "the son of Barakel the Buzite" (Job 32:2, 32:6), which means he descends from this man or that Buz was the name of his family region. He is the eponymous ancestor of the family or clan to which Elihu belongs, the young man who intervenes in Job's controversy.
H0940.origine: The name Buz means "contempt" or "disdain" in Hebrew, although no direct link is established in the text with Elihu's character. Buz is known as a region or clan in antiquity, probably in northern Arabia. The name also appears in the genealogy of Nahor, Abraham's brother, in Genesis 22:21, suggesting a people or tribe established during the patriarchal era.
H0940.emploi: Buz is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Job in chapter 32, where Elihu specifically presents himself as belonging to this lineage. The two identical occurrences indicate that it is an important genealogical detail for establishing Elihu's identity and origin, the young man who speaks after Job and his three friends have exhausted their debate on suffering and divine justice.

sens: Father of the prophet Ezekiel
H0941.detail: Buzi is the father of the prophet Ezekiel, mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 1:3. He lived during the time of the Babylonian exile. Ezekiel is presented as "the son of Buzi, the priest," indicating that Buzi was himself a priest or of priestly lineage. It is through this brief mention that we know of his existence: no other details about his life are reported in Scripture.
H0941.origine: The name Buzi literally means "my contempt" in Hebrew. Although its meaning is not flattering, the name reflects the Hebrew practice of giving names laden with theological or personal significance, often related to the circumstances of birth or the feelings of the parents.
H0941.emploi: Buzi appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 1:3, as the father of Ezekiel. He lived among the exiles of Judah in Babylonian territory, near the Kebar River, at the time when God called his son to prophetic mission. Although his personal life remains in the shadows, the fact that his name is preserved underscores the importance of his lineage with the great prophet who conveyed the words of the Lord to exiled Israel.

sens: Man who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah
District chief responsible for his area during the reconstruction
H0942.detail: 1. Bavvaï is a man who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, during the time of Nehemiah. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:18, where it is noted that he was the son of Henadad and worked on the wall construction site. 2. He held a position of authority: he was the chief of half the district of Keilah, which means he supervised the work in his geographical area and that the workers from his region worked under his direction during this great reconstruction.
H0942.origine: The name Bavvaï literally means "my paths" or "my passages," an expression that evokes movement and way. His father was Henadad, who was also involved in the reconstruction work. The name may reflect the idea of someone who "comes and goes," who moves and acts — a fitting quality for a foreman.
H0942.emploi: Bavvaï appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:18. He is listed among the many workers and leaders who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem in the 440s B.C., after the return of the exiles from Babylon. His name appears in the detailed list of sections of the wall and the teams responsible for them. The context shows that he worked with his brothers and other teams to accomplish this monumental task, under the general supervision of Nehemiah.

sens: To be lost, astray, or disoriented in a space
H0943.detail:
1. To be lost or astray in a space: the word describes the state of one who no longer knows where they are or how to orient themselves. In Exodus 14:3, Pharaoh says that the children of Israel are "lost" in the desert, as if they had lost their way.
2. To be troubled, confused, or dismayed in the face of a situation: this is an inner turmoil, a loss of bearings in front of a disturbing event. In Esther 3:15, the city of Susa is in "dismay" when the threatening decree is announced, caught between confusion and worry.
3. To groan or lament under the effect of confusion and distress: the word can express the complaint of one who is troubled or without resources. In Joel 1:18, the animals "groan" because they are dismayed, deprived of pasture and without hope.
H0943.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of confusion and disorientation. The word is primarily used in the niphal form (passive or reflexive), which emphasizes the state of one who undergoes confusion rather than the action of confusing someone else. The basic image is that of someone who has lost their bearings, whether spatial (no longer finding their way) or mental (no longer understanding a situation).
H0943.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to express a loss of orientation or understanding. In Exodus 14:3, it describes the supposed state of the Israelites in the desert according to Pharaoh's calculation: they seem lost, which could make them vulnerable. In Esther 3:15, it characterizes the turmoil and fear that grips the Persian capital in response to the king's decree. In Joel 1:18, it even applies to animals, which express through their cries a form of distress and confusion. In all cases, the word underscores a deep disturbance, whether physical, mental, or emotional.
H0943.portee: This word reminds us that disorientation and confusion can strike human beings and even all of creation in the face of trials or threats. For the believer, it invites recognition of these moments of darkness and anxiety as real and legitimate, while maintaining the confidence that God does not abandon us in confusion, even when everything seems lost.

sens: grass or vegetation that grows spontaneously and serves as food for animals
food, nourishment in general
that which feeds on something, that which lives from it
H0944.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of grass and greenery that animals find to eat in fields and mountains: in Job 40:15, the hippopotamus "finds its pasture in the mountains, where all the beasts of the field play" — it is the grass and plants it grazes in its natural habitat.
2. The word extends to any food or nourishment, any piece that one feeds on: in Isaiah 44:19, the foolish idolater "would bow down before a piece of wood," as if this remnant of material had value as food or sustenance — here the word simply denotes a portion, what remains of something consumed.
3. By extension, pasture can metaphorically designate what nourishes the soul or what something lives from: the pasture then becomes an image of what supports, what sustains life or activity.
H0944.origine: The Hebrew word בּוּל (bul) comes from a root that evokes growth and the production of vegetation. It is related to words meaning "to produce" and "to grow," and refers to the idea of what multiplies naturally. The word primarily designates the products of the soil — the grass that grows — before extending to any food that comes from it.
H0944.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible: once in Job 40:15 where it literally describes the natural food of the hippopotamus in the mountains, and once in Isaiah 44:19 where it denotes a piece of wood remaining after burning. In this second case, the context of idolatry slightly changes the tone: the word loses its connotation of living substance to become mere waste, an unnecessary fragment. Both usages show how the word shifts from the concrete (grass, food) to material concrete (piece, remnant).
H0944.portee: This word reminds us that every creature, even the largest and most powerful like the hippopotamus described by Job, depends on what creation produces for it. It invites recognition of divine providence in the food and support of life. In Isaiah, it underscores the absurdity of idolatry: to worship a mere piece of waste wood is to confuse the useless fragment with the source of life.

sens: Eighth month of the Hebrew calendar
Period corresponding to October-November or November-December according to the Gregorian calendar
H0945.detail: 1. Bul is the eighth month of the ancient Hebrew calendar, the one used by the Israelites before the exile. Its name evokes the idea of growth and production, as it was a season when crops developed. 2. This month generally corresponds to the end of autumn and the beginning of winter in our modern calendar, approximately October-November or November-December depending on the years. It is the time when the temple of Solomon was completed: "in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished" (1 Kings 6:38).
H0945.origine: The name Bul literally means "growth" or "production" in Hebrew, reflecting the agricultural activity and productivity of this time of year. After the Babylonian exile, the Hebrews adopted the Babylonian calendar and replaced this name with the Aramaic name "Marchesvan," which has remained in use in Judaism to this day.
H0945.emploi: The word Bul appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 6:38, where it designates the precise moment of the completion of the temple built by King Solomon. This unique usage shows that it is an ancient term, used in the ancient historical tradition of Israel before the calendar was renewed after the Babylonian exile. The use of this archaic name emphasizes the antiquity of the narrative and its roots in the early times of the united kingdom.
H0945.portee: This month reminds us that in the Old Testament, time was marked by sacred and agricultural rhythms distinct from our own. The completion of the temple in the month of Bul marks a decisive moment in the history of God's people: the house of prayer and divine presence was now ready, as the fruit of seven years of labor according to divine will.

sens: son of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah
H0946.detail: Buna is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the genealogies of Judah. He is the son of Jerahmeel and is part of the lineage of Judean family leaders during the time of the united monarchy in Israel.
H0946.origine: The name Buna means "intelligence" in Hebrew, likely derived from a root expressing wisdom or understanding. It carries the idea of discernment, an important value in Hebrew tradition.
H0946.emploi: Buna appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:25, in the genealogical list of the sons of Jerahmeel. He is listed among his brothers Ram, Oren, Otsem, Ahijah, and Onam. These genealogical lists, though discreet, serve to establish the continuity of the Davidic lineage and the importance of Judean families.

sens: To walk on something, to tread on it with the feet
To crush an enemy in battle, to defeat them
To reject with contempt, to treat indignantly
To defile or profane something sacred
H0947.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to walk on something, to tread on it: it is the physical action of crushing underfoot. Isaiah 63:6 says, "I trampled down peoples in my anger": the image is that of an army crushing the enemy underfoot, as one treads grapes to extract juice.
2. In battle, to trample means to defeat and crush militarily: the psalmist sings, "With you we push back our enemies; in your name we trample down our adversaries" (Psalms 44:6), expressing the overwhelming victory that God grants.
3. The word also expresses rejection and contempt: one who is "trampled underfoot" is treated as refuse, without dignity. Isaiah 14:19 describes the corpse of a defeated enemy, "trampled underfoot" in a pit.
4. Finally, to trample can mean to defile or profane: in Ezekiel 16:22, where the text uses "bathed" (a variant of the same verb), it refers to defiling someone with blood or treating them indignantly, which approaches the idea of dishonoring.
H0947.origine: The Hebrew verb bus comes from a root expressing the action of walking or treading. The family of the word includes the idea of foot movement. The verb appears in several grammatical forms in Hebrew, each nuance of the action: the simple form describes the action of trampling, while other forms reinforce or modify the meaning (rejection, profanation). This root is typically Semitic and expresses a concrete action that has become metaphorically powerful.
H0947.emploi: The verb to trample appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. It is frequently used in military contexts: Psalms 44:6 and 108:14 invoke God's ability to crush enemies. Isaiah uses it to describe divine judgment on nations (Isaiah 63:6) and the profanation of holy places (Isaiah 63:18). Jeremiah 12:10 uses it to describe how enemies ravage and trample the people of God. The context oscillates between military victory, divine judgment, and the indignity inflicted on the defeated.
H0947.portee: This verb helps the believer understand how the Bible speaks of victory and judgment: to trample means both to triumph with force and to inflict a humiliating defeat. It sheds light on how Scripture envisions divine justice and the defeat of God's enemies, not abstractly but with images of concrete and definitive victory. It is also a call to recognize God's power in the face of evil.

sens: Fine white fabric of linen woven in Egypt
Garment of dignity worn during religious ceremonies
Prestigious material for the decoration of sacred or royal spaces
Symbol of wealth and honor
H0948.detail:
1. Byssus is a precious white fabric, made in Egypt. It is a very fine and very white linen, crafted artfully by specialized artisans. In 1 Chronicles 4:21, we see entire families working with byssus as a trade.
2. Kings and priests wear byssus during major ceremonies. David dons a robe of byssus when the Ark of the Covenant is brought to Jerusalem, and the Levitical singers do the same (1 Chronicles 15:27; 2 Chronicles 5:12). It is a garment that shows the status and holiness of the one who wears it.
3. Byssus is used in the making of the Temple veil (2 Chronicles 3:14) and in the decoration of royal palaces (Esther 1:6). Its white brilliance and fine texture make it a worthy fabric for the house of God and the dwellings of kings.
4. Possessing and wearing byssus is a certain sign of power and wealth. Huram-Abi, the master craftsman sent by Tyre, knows how to make byssus among other precious materials (2 Chronicles 2:14). It is a luxury item that only the great adorn themselves with.
H0948.origine: The Hebrew word "buts" comes from the Egyptian and Syro-Phoenician world: it is a fabric renowned in biblical times, resulting from a very refined weaving technique. Byssus literally refers to white linen, probably a special variety of Egyptian linen woven with extreme care. In ancient Greek, the same fabric is called "byssos." The word spread through all the ancient cultures that bordered Egypt, as it was a prestigious trade product. Byssus embodied not only material wealth but also craftsmanship and excellence.
H0948.emploi: The word "byssus" appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the accounts of Chronicles and the book of Esther. It refers either to a garment worn during ceremonies (David and the Levites in 1 Chronicles 15:27 and 2 Chronicles 5:12), or to a raw material worked by specialized artisans (1 Chronicles 4:21 and 2 Chronicles 2:14), or to luxurious adornment for worship or royal residence (the Temple veil in 2 Chronicles 3:14, the decoration of Xerxes' palace in Esther 1:6). Each time, byssus marks dignity, consecration, or splendor. Its use does not vary much: it is always a sign of prestige and purity.
H0948.portee: Byssus reminds the believer that God values beauty, excellence, and order in worship. Seeing byssus adorn the Temple or clothe those who served God (like David and the Levites) shows us that faith does not exclude the pursuit of dignity and nobility. It is also a call to understand that some things deserve our utmost effort — serving God deserves our best.

sens: Steep rock near Micmash in Israel
H0949.detail: Botsets is a rocky peak or steep rock formation located near the city of Micmash, in the land of Israel. Its name literally means "bright white" or "that shines," which likely evokes a white and shining rock, visible from afar. In 1 Samuel 14:4, this rock becomes an important geographical landmark: Jonathan and his armor-bearer must cross it to reach the Philistine camp. The text describes it as a "tooth of rock" — a sharp and distinctive formation in the landscape — facing another rock called Sene. These two natural peaks serve as a narrow and steep passage, a strategic place for a bold ambush.
H0949.origine: The Hebrew name Botsets comes from a root evoking whiteness and brightness: the white and shining stone was striking in the rocky landscape of the region of Benjamin. It is a place name that derives its name from its natural appearance, a common characteristic in biblical geography.
H0949.emploi: Botsets appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 14:4. It is a very precise location given during Jonathan's exploit: this young warrior crosses this difficult passage with only his armor-bearer, in the heart of the night, to go fight the Philistine army. The rock of Botsets is thus linked to an act of bravery and trust in God, showing how courage and faith can overcome seemingly impossible natural and military obstacles.
H0949.portee: Botsets reminds us that God leads His people through difficult terrains and trials. This steep rock symbolizes the obstacles that the believer must traverse, not by their own strength, but by relying on faith and obedience. The story of Jonathan invites us to see how the "narrow passages" of life can become the place of divine victory.

sens: action of emptying a place of its riches
state of desolation and emptiness
devastation, destruction
moral and spiritual ruin
H0950.detail:
1. Plunder is the act of completely emptying a place of everything of value — it is the moment when invaders take everything. In Nahum 2:11, the prophet cries, "They plunder!", showing the city of Nineveh stripped of its treasures and its inhabitants in a burst of destruction.
2. The word also evokes the resulting state: total emptiness, desolation. A plundered city is nothing more than an empty space, where nothing remains of what constituted its wealth and life.
3. Plunder is complete destruction: not only is everything taken, but it is ravaged, broken, consumed. Nahum describes it amidst a picture of total chaos where "hearts are crushed, knees tremble".
4. Spiritually, the word also carries the image of inner emptiness: the soul stripped, emptied of its assurance and strength, in the face of God's judgment.
H0950.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to empty," "to make empty." It is formed on the concrete idea of the nothingness that remains after everything that filled a space has been removed. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, which underscores its dramatic weight when Nahum uses it to describe the punishment of Nineveh.
H0950.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Nahum 2:11. The prophet Nahum, speaking of the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, uses this term to evoke the total invasion of the city. It is a cry of alarm, a warning of the judgment that God sends against imperial power: everything that the empire has accumulated and of which it has boasted will be emptied, taken away, reduced to nothing. The context shows that this plunder is not merely a military spoil, but a sign of divine judgment that strikes even the hearts of the inhabitants.
H0950.portee: This image of plunder and emptiness reminds the believer that no earthly wealth, no human power is stable in the face of God. It also speaks of a salutary fear: one who unjustly accumulates or oppresses risks losing everything. But it also invites one to seek true riches, those that cannot be plundered — wisdom, justice, a relationship with God.

sens: One who keeps and pastures the flock
Field worker who raises livestock
H0951.detail:
1. The shepherd is one who keeps the sheep or livestock and pastures them. It is a humble profession, tied to pastoral and rural life. Amos proclaims that he is neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet, but simply a shepherd — a field worker who earns his living by caring for animals (Amos 7:14).
2. More broadly, the word designates a man of the fields, a pastor engaged in raising livestock, sometimes associated with other agricultural work: Amos adds that he also cultivates sycamores. It is the profession of the people, far from the cities and official religious institutions.
H0951.origine: The Hebrew word בּוֹקֵר (boqer) comes from a root that means "to keep" or "to watch over." It designates one who pastures the flock — the guardian of the animals. It is also found in other Hebrew forms related to livestock and pastoral life. It is a simple, concrete word, rooted in the daily life of the ancient Near East.
H0951.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in the mouth of the prophet Amos. Amos responds to Amaziah, the priest of the sanctuary of Bethel, affirming his humble and rural identity: he has not received official prophetic training, he is not from a dynasty of prophets, but he is a shepherd. This statement highlights the contrast between his simple condition and the divine call he has received — God pulls him from his flocks to make him His spokesperson. The word carries a strong charge: what might seem like a disqualification in the eyes of the established clergy becomes, in biblical logic, a guarantee of authenticity.
H0951.portee: Amos teaches us that God does not only call the learned and the notable: He can seize a simple man, a field worker, and transform him into a powerful prophet. This word invites the believer not to despise the small and to recognize that God often acts through those whom the world considers insignificant. It also frees those who feel without social or religious qualifications: God looks at the heart and obedience, not status.

sens: Subject to careful, scrutinizing examination
Explore a question in depth to gain clarity
H0952.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of looking closely at something, applying one's attention methodically — as one explores or probes a matter to unravel its nature. In Ecclesiastes 9:1, the wise man says, "I have applied my heart to all this; I have made it the object of my examination": it is the intelligent effort of someone seeking to understand the mysteries of the world and the human condition.
2. The word also carries the idea of clarification: by examining things, one seeks to make them clear, to unravel their meaning — not a simple passive observation, but an investigation that aspires to pierce what is obscure or hidden.
H0952.origine: The Hebrew root בּוּר (bur) appears infrequently in the Old Testament and remains partially enigmatic regarding its original image. Some connections suggest an idea of separation or distinction, and thus by extension of clarification: to examine is to separate, discriminate, make clear. The context of Ecclesiastes, a book of sapiential reflection, where only one use is known to us, confirms this orientation towards intelligent inquiry.
H0952.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ecclesiastes 9:1. The Ecclesiastes, this book of the wise man's reflections, uses it to describe his approach: he has applied himself to examine all the phenomena of the world — the fate of the righteous and the wise, the place of love and hate, human endeavors. It is a word from someone who has conducted a comprehensive investigation, a quest for meaning in the face of the enigmas of existence. The text shows that this meticulous examination leads to a conclusion: the righteous and the wise are in the hand of God, but men know nothing of their true destinies.
H0952.portee: This word invites us to meditate on the value of careful examination — not as vain curiosity, but as a heart's endeavor that seeks to understand God's hand in our lives. It also reminds us of the humility of the wise: the more one examines things deeply, the more one discovers what one does not know. To examine is not to accumulate answers, but to learn to ask the right questions before God.

sens: Reservoir dug in the ground or rock to collect and store rainwater
Well or water source
Deep pit, natural or dug, often underground
Prison or dungeon where captives are held
Figuratively, death or the realm of the dead, the abyss of destruction
H0953A.detail:
1. A cistern is a reservoir intentionally dug to store water, especially in dry regions where water is precious. In Leviticus 11:36, it is said that "the springs and the cisterns, forming pools of water, shall remain clean," as they hold the water of life. In 2 Chronicles 26:10, the king digs "many cisterns" for his livestock: it is a wealth, an investment.
2. The cistern can also simply refer to a well or a water source. Proverbs 5:15 invokes the poetic image: "Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well."
3. An empty cistern becomes a pit—a deep, dark hole. In Genesis 37:20-24, Joseph's brothers throw him "into one of the cisterns": it is a pit without water where he sinks into the mud, as in Jeremiah 38:6.
4. This naturally prison-like pit literally becomes a dungeon where captives are held: Jeremiah is "thrown into the cistern" to die. It is a place of detention and suffering.
5. Figuratively, the cistern or pit becomes the image of death, the abyss, the realm of the dead. In Ezekiel 26:20, God casts the city "with those who have gone down into the pit," evoking the eternal fate of the lost. In Psalms 28:1, one cries "to the pit"—on the brink of death.
H0953A.origine: The Hebrew word bor comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to pierce." It is a concrete noun: it designates what is dug into the ground. The word is used throughout the Hebrew Bible, from the most mundane (household water) to the most dramatic (imprisonment, death). It has no major cognates in Hebrew but expresses the universal idea of hollow and depth.
H0953A.emploi: This word appears about 60 times in the Old Testament, in all genres: history, law, poetry, prophecy. In its primary senses (water reservoir, source), the uses are concrete and practical: cisterns are dug for drinking, washing, watering livestock (Genesis, Exodus, 2 Chronicles). Early on, the empty cistern becomes an image of misfortune: throwing someone into a cistern means condemning them to death (Genesis 37 with Joseph). In poetry and prophecy, the pit rises to designate the realm of the dead, the abyss: Psalms and Ezekiel use it to express extreme distress, the fear of oblivion and death. Jeremiah literally suffers in a cistern-prison (Jeremiah 38), where the word combines all its meanings: dungeon, hole, threat of death.
H0953A.portee: For the Christian reading this word, it first evokes the biblical image of life and death. Living water is salvation, the gift of God; the empty cistern is danger, abandonment, spiritual death. Jesus will take up this image by promising "living water" to the Samaritan woman (John 4), contrasting the stagnant water of our own wells with the life-giving gift of the Father. Reading that Jeremiah sinks into the mud of a cistern reminds us that even the prophet suffers, and that only God can pull from the abyss.

sens: Reservoir dug in the ground or rock to collect and store rainwater
Place for storage and reserve of water in arid regions
H0953B.detail:
1. A cistern is a large reservoir dug in the ground or in the rock, which serves to collect and store rainwater. In Palestine, where water is precious and sources are rare, cisterns are essential for survival. The cistern of Sira, mentioned in 2 Samuel 3:26, is a known and identifiable place, significant enough to serve as a geographical landmark.
2. By extension, the cistern represents a place of safety and resource: the water it contains allows life during dry periods. This is why it also becomes a symbol of what sustains and preserves life.
H0953B.origine: The Hebrew word בּוֹר (bor) primarily denotes a hole, a dug pit. The cistern is its most common practical application in the ancient East: the ground or rock is dug to collect rainwater, a vital resource in semi-arid regions. This word belongs to a broad semantic field including any excavation or cavity, which emphasizes the aspect of "digging" at the origin of the concept.
H0953B.emploi: The word בּוֹר appears only once in this passage from 2 Samuel 3:26. The cistern of Sira is mentioned as a specific and known place, where Joab sent messengers to bring Abner back to David. It serves as a geographical reference in the narrative, showing that cisterns, as permanent and important structures, served as landmarks in the Palestinian landscape. The usage here is factual and geographical.
H0953B.portee: This modest mention reminds us that life in the biblical land depends on the careful management of water. It invites the reader to meditate on the fragility and preciousness of vital resources, as well as the wisdom required to survive in a demanding environment. It also highlights how God provides for the needs of His people even in aridity.

sens: To feel shame, embarrassment, or discomfort in a situation
To be confused, disappointed, or discouraged by a failure, defeat, or unmet expectation
To be brought into disgrace or public discredit
To act or behave in a shameful or unworthy manner
H0954.detail:
1. To feel shame means to experience embarrassment or discomfort. In the simplest sense, the man and woman in the Garden of Eden "were both naked and were not ashamed" (Genesis 2:25), for there was no guilt or shame between them. It is this feeling that makes you blush or lower your eyes.
2. To be confused or disappointed expresses a state of dejection or disillusionment: when your hopes collapse, when your plans fail, you are "ashamed." The psalmist cries: "Let me not be put to shame when I call upon you" (Psalms 31:18), fearing that his trust in God may be contradicted by events.
3. To be brought into disgrace or reproach means to lose honor and dignity publicly, as when God "shames" the enemies of Israel. Psalms 35:4 asks that the adversaries "be ashamed and dishonored."
4. To act shamefully or without modesty means to conduct oneself in a way that deserves shame. Jeremiah reproaches the wicked: "They are not ashamed; they do not know how to blush" (Jeremiah 8:12), denouncing their moral insensitivity and lack of remorse.
H0954.origine: The verb הבוש comes from a root that expresses the idea of feeling uncomfortable, retreating, or turning away. The word also appears in forms that mean "to be discouraged" or "disappointed." The word family includes the noun "shame" (בּוֹשֶׁת) and the adjective "ashamed" (בּוֹשׁ). The biblical context shows that shame is related to the loss of honor, the failure to fulfill promises, or moral guilt.
H0954.emploi: This verb appears more than 110 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms (where the psalmist asks God to preserve him from shame and to "confound" his enemies), in the Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah), and in the Wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs). It designates both the personal feeling of shame and the action of "shaming" someone: God can shame idols and their worshipers, or preserve His faithful from confusion. The verb enriches with a moral nuance: to be ashamed can mean a healthy remorse, but "not blushing" for one's sins expresses the hardening of the heart. Isaiah 29:22 promises that Jacob "shall not be ashamed anymore" because the Lord has redeemed him: this is an assurance of restoration and future honor.
H0954.portee: Understanding this word helps the believer grasp the biblical dialectic between shame and honor. The shame of sin is a step toward repentance when it creates healthy remorse; but God promises that those who trust in Him will not be "ashamed"—this is a certainty of deliverance and justification. This word invites us not to harden our conscience by refusing to acknowledge our faults, and to trust that the Lord will lift us up.

sens: painful feeling of dishonor or ridicule in relation to oneself or others
state of one who is publicly humiliated or dishonored
covering, enveloping that denotes confusion and disarray
H0955.detail:
1. Shame is primarily that painful feeling that seizes someone when they feel dishonored or ridiculed. It is a deep emotion related to the loss of dignity. It can be provoked by one's own actions or by what one suffers: this is what the enemy of God feels in Micah 7:10, who "will be covered with shame" when their reproaches turn against them.
2. Shame also refers to the visible state of public humiliation and dishonor. It is not just an inner feeling: it manifests, it "covers" someone like a garment. In Ezekiel 7:18, shame envelops the confused faces of people filled with terror, showing how misfortune inscribes confusion on their very features.
3. In certain contexts, shame takes on a broader hue: it is the atmosphere of confusion and disarray that descends upon someone. In Obadiah 1:10, Edom "will be covered with shame" for its violence, which evokes not only humiliation but also the total collapse of its glory.
H0955.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "to cover" and refers to a concrete image: just as one veils their face or wraps themselves when they are ashamed. This primary sense of veiling or covering remains alive in biblical usages, where shame "covers" or "envelops" the person. It is a visible, manifest shame, not hidden in secret.
H0955.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic and poetic books. In Psalms 89:46, David prays to God, recalling how he has "covered" the king with shame — it is an affront to the dignity of the people. Among the prophets (Ezekiel, Obadiah, Micah), shame is one of the consequences of divine judgment or God's justice: it strikes the violent (Obadiah 1:10), it envelops the terrified people (Ezekiel 7:18), it rewards the enemy of the oppressed (Micah 7:10). Each time, it is a covering that is visible, marking publicly the one who bears it.
H0955.portee: This word reminds us that in the eyes of God and in the Bible, dishonor and humiliation are real and serious. It is not just a psychological wound: it is a social and spiritual reality. For the believer, shame also evokes the importance of living uprightly, for pride and violence inevitably lead to public confusion. But it is also a call to mercy: one who confesses their shame before God can be restored.

sens: Stay somewhere overnight to sleep or rest
Temporarily reside in a place
H0956.detail:
1. To spend the night means to sleep or stay awake in a place during the nighttime hours. King Darius, in Daniel 6:18, "spends" the night in his palace, fasting and sleepless, worried about Daniel thrown into the lion's den. The word simply evokes the action of remaining in a place overnight.
2. More broadly, it means to stay or lodge somewhere, even temporarily. It is the nighttime rest that gives it meaning: one spends the night where they rest or where they await dawn.
H0956.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew "bayit" (בַּ֫יִת), which means "house" or "dwelling." The link is clear: to spend the night is to be lodged, to remain in a house. Aramaic and Hebrew share this close vocabulary, reflecting the kinship of the two ancient Near Eastern languages.
H0956.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 6:18. It is a specific Aramaic form found in the book of Daniel, which dates from the period of Persian domination and widely uses Aramaic. In this royal context, the king "spends the night" in his palace, which underscores both his place of residence and his state of anxious insomnia: he does not sleep, he watches.
H0956.portee: This passage reminds us that even a powerful king knows anxiety and insomnia in the face of injustice. Darius spends a sleepless night because he regrets condemning Daniel, whom he recognizes as just. For the reader, it is a moment where earthly power is measured against the power of God: the king can neither sleep nor act, while Daniel is preserved in the den.

sens: that which is taken by force from a defeated enemy
the goods of a person or nation that become the possession of the victor
the act of seizing violently
the condition of one who becomes a victim, an easy prey
H0957.detail: 1. Plunder primarily refers to the totality of goods and riches seized by force during a military victory: loot, treasure taken in battle. When Israel enters Canaan, the Israelites fear that their women and children may become a "prey" in the hands of enemies (Numbers 14:3). 2. This word also applies to the very act of seizing, of violently appropriating. The Lord distributes the plunder that Moses takes from the Midianites (Numbers 31:32). 3. Plunder can refer to the state of vulnerability, when something or someone becomes exposed to being taken. Israel becomes a "prey" when it turns away from God (Jeremiah 2:14). 4. By extension, the word expresses the idea of exploitation, of dispossession. Ezekiel promises that God's flock will no longer be "plundered" among the nations, meaning it will no longer be delivered to those who persecute it (Ezekiel 34:28).
H0957.origine: The Hebrew root originally means "to tear away," "to remove." The word evokes the action of seizing by force, of stripping. It is found in military contexts and in that of violated property rights. The basic image is that of a warrior seizing the goods of the defeated and carrying them away.
H0957.emploi: This word appears twenty-five times in the Old Testament, particularly in the prophetic books of Ezekiel (thirteen occurrences) and Jeremiah. It is used in contexts of war, divine judgment, and oppression. Plunder describes the consequences of sin: when Israel disobeys, it becomes "booty" and "prey" for its enemies (2 Kings 21:14). It is a concrete term that anchors divine punishment in a material and human reality. The word also applies to animals: the camels of the Midianites will be "plundered" (Jeremiah 49:32). God promises the end of plunder as a sign of restoration and salvation: His sheep will cease to be a "prey" of the nations (Ezekiel 34:22, 34:28).
H0957.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that sin has concrete and serious consequences: it makes us vulnerable to destruction and loss. But it also teaches that God does not abandon us without recourse. The promise that we will no longer be "plundered" offers the hope of divine protection, of security restored in God. It is a word of comfort for those who suffer under oppression.

sens: To slice, divide by passing through
To share a territory by crossing it
H0958.detail:
1. The verb "to cut" refers to the action of slicing or dividing something by passing through it cleanly. It is a physical, concrete action: one cuts as one would split wood with an axe or a knife that passes through the material.
2. In both usages in Isaiah 18, the word describes how the rivers "cut" through the land of Cush (ancient Ethiopia): they divide it, traversing it and sharing it into distinct sections. The rivers thus create a network that structures the territory.
H0958.origine: The Hebrew verb bazá comes from a root expressing the idea of dividing or cutting in two. It is a simple and concrete word, painting the image of a blade or a current passing through a surface. The biblical context shows that it mainly applies to what cleaves space: water that cuts, a boundary that divides.
H0958.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, in verses 2 and 7 of Isaiah 18, in a description of the land of Cush. It specifically qualifies how the rivers "cut" or "divide" this region.
