It is a geographical and descriptive usage: the biblical poet borrows this vocabulary of physical division to evoke the river network that structures the territory. The usage remains limited and specialized.
H0958.portee: This word reminds us that geography is not neutral in the biblical vision: rivers and natural boundaries organize the world. For the reader, it invites us to see in the created order — the waters, the lands — an intelligible partition, a signature of divine wisdom.

sens: to reject with contempt, to regard as worthless
to treat with disdain, to consider unworthy
to be or become despicable, unworthy
to treat someone by pushing them to contempt
H0959.detail:
1. To despise means to look at something or someone with deep contempt, as if they are worth nothing. It is a rejection that comes from the heart: Esau "despised" his birthright (Genesis 25:34) by exchanging it for a simple meal, showing that he considered it of little value. The psalmist, on the other hand, looks "with disdain at the one who is despicable" (Psalms 15:4), refusing to honor him.
2. To despise also means to treat someone or something with disdain, to dismiss, to reject as unworthy. King David offended the Lord by acting wickedly, and the Lord said: "you have despised me" (2 Samuel 12:10), meaning that David had willfully set Him aside in his heart.
3. To be despicable means to be or become worthy of contempt, worthless or dishonorable. The psalmist cries: "I am small and despised" (Psalms 119:141), expressing his humiliation and degradation.
4. To cause contempt is to push someone to contempt: Ezekiel reproaches Jerusalem for "despising" the sanctuaries of God (Ezekiel 22:8), meaning treating them without respect, which gives rise to contempt towards them.
H0959.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּזָה comes from a root that expresses rejection and disdain. It is a concrete word at its core: it denotes the act of turning away, of pushing away with the hand or with the heart. The family of the word includes notions of contempt and indignity. This verb is mainly used to describe attitudes of the human heart towards God, His ordinances, and His messengers, or towards people based on their honor or shame.
H0959.emploi: The verb "to despise" appears 42 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books, the psalms, the proverbs, and the prophets. It is used in three main ways. First, a man despises something concrete (an inheritance, an oath, a law): thus Esau despised his birthright by exchanging it for bread. Next, one despises a person: David despised the Lord by committing adultery, or Saul is despised by the "worthless men" who did not honor him (1 Samuel 10:27). Finally, one can be despised oneself: the suffering servant of the Messiah is "despised and forsaken by men" (Isaiah 53:3), a powerful image of humiliation and rejection. The prophets often reproach Israel for despising the Lord by not respecting His ordinances and His holy days.
H0959.portee: This word teaches us that contempt is an attitude of the heart that has serious consequences. When we despise God or His word, we push Him away from our lives, just as Esau rejected his blessing. Conversely, we understand the humiliation of the Messiah: He who is Lord accepted to be "despised and forsaken," to lift us from our indignity. The word calls us to respect God and not to despise the small or those who suffer, for God does not despise them.

sens: Goods, wealth taken by force from a defeated enemy
The act of stealing, ravaging, stripping
What is taken, seized, placed under the power of a conqueror
H0961.detail: 1. Plunder primarily refers to the totality of goods and wealth taken from a defeated enemy: this can include precious objects, livestock, money, anything of value. When the army of Judah defeats the enemy army, "the spoils were considerable" (2 Chronicles 14:13) — these are all the treasures they bring back from the battlefield. 2. The word also describes the act itself of stripping, plundering, ravaging cities: it is the action by which one forcibly removes. After a victory, the soldiers "took many spoils" (2 Chronicles 25:13), meaning they plundered, emptied the cities of their goods. 3. More broadly, plunder can refer to the state of devastation a country finds itself in after conquest: Israel fears being delivered "to plunder" (Ezra 9:7), meaning to be conquered and stripped of its wealth by a foreign power.
H0961.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of taking away, stealing, forcibly stripping. It is found in other words that speak of brigandage and theft. In Greek, the Septuagint (an ancient translation of the Bible into Greek) often translates it with words meaning "booty" or "what is taken away." It is a term from military and political language: it speaks of the fate of the defeated.
H0961.emploi: This word appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of Chronicles (history of the kings of Judah) and in the accounts of Esther and Daniel. It designates the wealth that victorious soldiers take from their enemies: when Amaziah sends away warriors, they plunder the cities of Judah and carry off spoils (2 Chronicles 25:13); after the victory over Haman, the Jews did not "lay their hands on the plunder" (Esther 9:10), which shows that they could have done so. The word is also used to speak of what a nation suffers when it is defeated: Israel dreads being delivered to plunder by foreign kings (Ezra 9:7). It is therefore a concrete term from the vocabulary of war.
H0961.portee: This word reminds us that war has real material consequences for those who are defeated. For an Israelite in exile, hearing about plunder evokes loss, ruin, dispossession — this is what happens when one turns away from God. Conversely, when Judah wins victory and takes booty, it is a sign that God blesses His people. Plunder is the concrete mark of God's judgment or grace upon the nations.

sens: To forcibly take the goods of a city, a people, especially after a military victory
To strip someone, to take away their possessions
To be reduced to plunder, to ruin
War booty; the totality of stolen or seized goods
H0962.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to seize by force the riches of a city or an enemy camp after a battle. It is the typical action of the victor who takes everything he can. In Genesis 34:27, the sons of Jacob plunder the city of Shechem after avenging their sister. In 2 Kings 7:16, the starving people of Samaria go out to plunder the camp of the Syrians who have fled. 2. The verb also means to strip someone of their goods, to reduce them to misery. Isaiah 42:22 speaks of Israel plundered and delivered to booty by the enemies of God. It is an act of injustice when it targets the innocent. 3. To be plundered means to become the prey of booty, to be reduced to nothing. Isaiah 24:3 announces that the land will be delivered to plunder according to the decree of the Lord: it is total ruin. 4. The word also designates the booty itself, the spoils seized. In Numbers 31:32-53, the booty from the victory over Midian is counted, divided between the people and the priests.
H0962.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּזַז (bazaz) expresses the idea of taking away, stripping with violence. The root evokes the action of taking and tearing apart. The noun בִּזָּה (bizah) derives from it, meaning "booty" or "spoil." In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often corresponds to the Greek διαρπάζω (diarpazo), which has the same meaning.
H0962.emploi: The verb appears 39 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and prophetic books. It regularly describes the action of victors over the defeated: Joshua and the Israelites plunder the Canaanite cities (Joshua 8:2, 27), Samson plunders the cities of the Philistines (Judges 14:19), the kings of Judah win spoils (2 Chronicles 14:13, 20:25). The word is also used in the passive voice to describe punishment: the prophets announce that Israel or Judah will be plundered by its enemies due to its unfaithfulness (Jeremiah 50:37, Ezekiel 38:12). In the Psalms (109:11), plunder symbolizes the ruin of the wicked.
H0962.portee: To plunder is never a neutral act in the Bible. When it is the conquest of the promised lands, plunder accompanies the will of God. But when it is the result of injustice or sin, plunder becomes punishment. For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that stolen riches never remain in the hands of the wicked, and that God watches over justice: He alone decides who will be exalted and who will be brought to nothing.

sens: The act of regarding someone or something as unworthy of respect or esteem
State of degradation or shame resulting from being treated without respect
Lack of consideration or honor towards a person
H0963.detail:
1. Contempt is the attitude of one who judges someone or something as unworthy of respect. It is a feeling of disdain, a form of rejection or disparagement. In Esther 1:18, when Queen Vashti refuses to obey the king, this act provokes "contempt" among the princesses of Persia and Media: they discuss it with all the officials, setting an example of disobedience that could spread a lack of respect for royal authority.
2. Contempt can also refer to the shameful and humiliating state of the one who is despised, the degradation they endure. It is less a feeling than a condition: to be covered with contempt is to be treated without honor and to suffer dishonor.
H0963.origine: The Hebrew word בִּזָּיוֹן (bizzayôn) comes from the root בזה (bazah), which means "to despise" or "to treat with disdain." This root evokes the idea of belittling, of considering something as insignificant. The word belongs to the family of verbs that express contempt or outrage, common in the wisdom literature and historical narratives of the Hebrew Bible.
H0963.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 1:18. It describes the social consequences of Queen Vashti's disobedience: her refusal to appear before the king creates a situation where respect for royal authority is at risk of being undermined. The context shows that contempt is a threat to social and political order, capable of spreading quickly among the subjects of the kingdom. It is a word chosen to express the serious stakes of this incident: the affront to the king's honor and to the hierarchy he represents.
H0963.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible recognizes contempt as a real force that destroys relationships and social order. It invites the reader to reflect on respect, dignity, and honor: how do we treat those we consider inferior? The story of Esther shows that contempt is never a private feeling without consequence — it spreads and shakes the foundations of a community.

sens: City in southern Judah near Beersheba
H0964.detail: Bizjothja is a small city located in southern Judah, near Beersheba. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the Promised Land (Joshua 15:28).
H0964.origine: The name Bizjothja literally means "contempt of Yahweh" or "the contempt looks at Yahweh." It is composed of two elements: "bizya" (contempt, outrage) and the divine name Yahweh. This type of composition was common in Hebrew place and personal names, where the religious context was inscribed in the toponymy itself.
H0964.emploi: Bizjothja appears only once in the Scriptures, in Joshua 15:28, in the description of the territory assigned to Judah. It is listed among the cities of the Negev, the desert region of southern Judah, between Hazor and Beersheba. This location confirms its role as a small settlement in a sparsely populated area of the southern desert.

sens: A flash that crosses the sky
The bright and sudden light of a flash
That which is dazzling, of extreme speed
H0965.detail:
1. Lightning is the natural phenomenon of a flash tearing through the sky — this intense and instantaneous band of light that bursts forth during storms. In Ezekiel 1:14, the prophet describes the creatures in his vision who "ran and returned like lightning," expressing their movement with lightning speed, without hesitation, comparable to the swiftness of a flash.
2. Beyond the physical flash, lightning evokes everything that is brilliant and breathtaking — a light that almost blinds by its intensity. It symbolizes the manifest divine power, the irresistible speed of God's action.
3. Lightning also figuratively denotes absolute speed and efficiency: that which occurs in an instant, without delay, with unwavering certainty.
H0965.origine: The Hebrew word bazaq is related to Semitic roots denoting brightness and brilliance. It paints the image of a luminous discharge that suddenly and spectacularly bursts from the sky. In the biblical universe, lightning is often associated with the manifestation of divine power and the theophany — when God reveals Himself visibly and majestically.
H0965.emploi: The word bazaq appears only once in the Greek New Testament (translated here as the Greek astre). In Ezekiel 1:14, it describes the dizzying movement of the celestial beings glimpsed in the prophet's vision: they go and return "like lightning," that is, with instantaneous obedience, supernatural agility. This context reveals how the Bible uses lightning to express what is divine, sovereign, and irresistible.
H0965.portee: For the believer, lightning reminds us that God acts with absolute power and swiftness. It invites us to recognize that His will is executed without delay, without obstacle, and to accept with confidence the rapidity of His interventions in our lives. It is an image of His transcendence and sovereign authority over all things.

sens: City of Canaan where Israel won a victory against the Canaanites and the Perizzites
Residence of Adonibezek, Canaanite king
H0966G.detail:
1. Bezek is a city in Canaan where, during the time of the Judges, the tribe of Judah and its allies won a decisive victory against the Canaanites and the Perizzites. It is there that Israel defeated ten thousand men (Judges 1:4), marking an important success in the conquest of the Promised Land.
2. Bezek is also the seat of Adonibezek, a Canaanite king who established his residence there. It is in this city that Israel found and fought this king (Judges 1:5), defeating and capturing him, which consolidated Israelite control of this region.
H0966G.origine: The name Bezek literally means "lightning" or "flash" in Hebrew, an evocative image for a strategic city. The name may evoke the speed and power of the victory won at this location, or the nature of the site itself. No other occurrence of the word appears in the Old Testament outside of these two passages in the book of Judges.
H0966G.emploi: Bezek appears twice in the Bible, both in the book of Judges, chapter 1. It is mentioned as the site of a major victory for Israel under the leadership of Judah: first as the place where ten thousand Canaanite fighters were defeated (Judges 1:4), and then as the seat of Adonibezek, the local king whom Israel fought and captured (Judges 1:5). These two references illustrate the strategic and military importance of this city during the initial conquest of Canaan.

sens: Gathering place of Israel's troops under Saul
H0966H.detail: Bezek is a locality where King Saul gathered the fighters of Israel for a military campaign. It is there that the three hundred thousand men of Israel and the thirty thousand men of Judah were counted (1 Samuel 11:8). The name evokes the idea of a flash or a glow, which suited a strategic place where troops mobilized quickly.
H0966H.origine: The Hebrew name Bezek derives from a root meaning "lightning" or "glow," an image of something that shines or bursts forth. This type of geographical name often reflects a natural characteristic of the place — perhaps its elevated or open position, where light struck. The same root appears in other biblical contexts related to brightness or fire.
H0966H.emploi: Bezek appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 11:8. It is during the reign of Saul, the first king of Israel, that Adonibezek, a Canaanite king, occupied this region. Saul gathered an impressive army there to fight the Ammonites and repel an enemy threat. The choice of this location for the gathering suggests an important strategic position in the Promised Land.

sens: Scatter, disorder
Break the unity or cohesion of a group
H0967.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of scattering, of putting into disorder. In Psalms 68:31, the psalmist asks God to "disperse" the warrior peoples, meaning to put them to flight, to separate them so that they no longer form a united threat.
2. Figuratively, it expresses the idea of breaking the unity or cohesion of a group: fragmenting forces, undoing an alliance or an army. It is asking God to weaken the enemy by disuniting them.
H0967.origine: The Hebrew root בזר (bzr) evokes the idea of dispersing or scattering. It appears only a few times in the Hebrew Bible, always with this nuance of putting into disorder or disseminating. The warrior and royal context in which it is used emphasizes its use in the language of psalms and prophecies.
H0967.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Bible. In Psalms 68:31, it is an invocation: the psalmist implores God to disperse the belligerent peoples who worship money and seek war. In Daniel 11:24, the political and military context shows how the kings of the East use cunning to disperse their enemies. The usage remains constantly attached to the idea of breaking an opposing unity, whether military or political.
H0967.portee: This word reminds us that the apparent strength of God's enemies is but an illusion: God can bring them to nothing by separating them. For the believer, this affirms that God controls history and the powers of the world, and that He can weaken those who oppose Him by breaking their cohesion. It is an invitation to trust in divine sovereignty.

sens: Eunuch in the service of King Ahasuerus
H0968.detail: Biztha is one of the seven eunuchs who served directly under King Ahasuerus (also known as Xerxes) at the Persian royal court. His name appears in the list of palace officials to whom the king gives orders during a royal feast on the seventh day of festivities. It was a position of trust and proximity to the sovereign.
H0968.origine: The name Biztha means "booty" or "spoil" in Hebrew, derived from a root evoking plunder or war gain. This meaning of the name contrasts with the political and administrative role he held at the Persian court, where eunuchs served as high-ranking officers.
H0968.emploi: Biztha is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Esther 1:10. He is among the seven eunuchs named to whom King Ahasuerus commands to summon Queen Vashti during a royal feast. His inclusion in this list indicates his importance as a court servant and recalls the hierarchical structure of the Achaemenid palace. The names of the seven eunuchs are all of Persian origin or inspiration, reflecting the historical context of the book of Esther.

sens: One who examines and judges the quality of something
One who scrutinizes and tests metals to verify their purity
Figuratively, one who observes and evaluates people's behavior
H0969.detail: 1. This word originally denotes the skilled worker who examines precious metals to test their quality and purity — the "assayer" or metal inspector. In Jeremiah 6:27, God says to Jeremiah: "I have made you a tester among my people," meaning that Jeremiah is constituted as one who examines, scrutinizes, judges the heart and behavior of people. 2. The underlying image is that of a tester, one who sifts, who puts to the test to discern what is good from what is bad. 3. Applied to men, the word expresses the mission of vigilant observation and discernment: to observe, probe, evaluate with wisdom and authority.
H0969.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to test," "to prove," "to examine." It is related to other biblical terms concerning testing and judgment. The primary image is that of the artisan who tests metals by fire or other means to verify their quality — an activity that requires expertise and discernment.
H0969.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 6:27. God entrusts the prophet Jeremiah with a mission of "observation" among His people: he must examine their ways, probe their behavior, like an inspector tests metals. This is a difficult and solitary mission — Jeremiah is established to discern and report, to be a witness to the moral and spiritual reality of Israel. This unique occurrence reveals the prophetic function itself: to observe, test, judge.
H0969.portee: This word reminds the reader that the prophet, and more broadly, one who speaks on behalf of God, is a vigilant observer of human life. For the Christian, it also evokes that God Himself probes the hearts (Jeremiah 17:10) with divine expertise, and that He expects His servants to have faithful discernment between good and evil.

sens: Boy or man in early adolescence or early adulthood
Vigorous and valiant warrior, particularly in a military context
Handsome and elegant man, often admired for his appearance
Figure of vigor, physical strength, and vitality
H0970.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a boy or young man, at the age where he leaves childhood without yet reaching adult maturity. It is the age of growth and physical development: in Ecclesiastes 12:1, the young man is urged to remember his Creator in the days of his youth.
2. In war and combat narratives, the word takes on a military dimension and specifically denotes the young and vigorous warrior, one who possesses the strength and endurance to fight. Psalms 78:31 describes how God "struck down the young men of Israel," and Isaiah 31:8 speaks of the "young warriors" of the Assyrians who will be enslaved.
3. The word can also emphasize the beauty and physical appeal of the young man. In Ezekiel 23:12, the "young and charming" Assyrian horsemen captivated by their elegance and vigor.
4. Beyond biological age, the word evokes vigor and vital strength: in Proverbs 20:29, "the glory of young men is their strength," expressing the idea that youth is the time of physical power and dynamism.
H0970.origine: The Hebrew word בָּחוּר (bachur) comes from a root that evokes the idea of choosing or selecting. The young man is one who is "chosen" — in a sense, one who stands out, who has been elected or separated by his vigor and qualities. This etymology aligns well with the use of the word to denote choice warriors and elite fighters. The word appears 43 times in the Old Testament, primarily in historical, poetic, and prophetic books.
H0970.emploi: The word regularly appears in contexts of war and catastrophe: Jeremiah laments several times how young men are struck down by the sword in battle (Jeremiah 18:21, 51:22), and Lamentations lists young men among the victims of the destruction of Jerusalem (Lamentations 1:15, 2:21). It also appears in passages of blessing and ordinary life: Joel 2:28 announces that the Spirit will be poured out on young men, Psalms 148:12 calls them to praise the Lord, and Ruth 3:10 describes Boaz as a "man of valor." The word regularly emphasizes physical strength: in 1 Samuel 9:2, Saul is presented as a young man "strong and handsome," and Isaiah 40:30 reminds that even young men grow weary.
H0970.portee: This word invites the believer to situate themselves in the cycle of life and to recognize the responsibility attached to youth. It is a time of strength and capacity to serve God, but also a time when one is exposed to dangers and temptations. Ecclesiastes 12:1 reminds us that it is in youth that one should turn to their Creator. Furthermore, the numerous passages that speak of young men struck in war warn us that physical vigor is not a guarantee of survival: only trust in God offers true protection.

sens: A tall structure made of stone or wood, intended for attack or defense
Fortress or bastion of a city
Construction used for lookout or surveillance
H0971.detail:
1. The word refers to a siege tower, a mobile or built structure constructed during an assault to dominate the enemy walls and get closer — a formidable weapon of war. In Isaiah 23:13, the Chaldeans raise towers against Tyre to overthrow its palaces: it is an instrument of massive attack, demonstrating the military power of the one who builds them.
2. The word can also refer to a fortified tower, part of a city's defenses, which serves to protect and control the territory.
3. More broadly, it is a tall construction used for lookout, from which one watches for approaches and defends.
H0971.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of encircling, surrounding, hence the meaning of that which encircles or dominates a space. The word belongs to the vocabulary of fortification and war, common in the Bible to describe the defensive constructions of ancient peoples.
H0971.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 23:13, in a passage where the prophet describes the assault of the Chaldeans against the city of Tyre. The "towers" he speaks of are siege engines, military constructions intended to overcome the walls of the enemy city. This passage shows the destructive power of Babylon by illustrating its war techniques.
H0971.portee: This word reminds us that human powers, even those equipped with impressive military means, remain instruments in the hand of God. In Isaiah, it is God who allows or limits conquests; the tower, no matter how high, can do nothing against divine will.

sens: One whom God has chosen for a particular mission or covenant
One who belongs to the people chosen by God
One who enjoys God's special favor
H0972.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a person whom God has personally chosen to accomplish an important task or to receive a promise: Moses is the chosen one who intercedes for the threatened people (Psalms 106:23), and David is the chosen one with whom God made a covenant (Psalms 89:4). It is a deliberate and free divine choice.
2. It also applies to the entire people of Israel, whom God has set apart for Himself: His chosen ones are called to possess the land and to serve it (Isaiah 65:9 and 65:22). The election is collective, marking belonging to God's project.
3. Ultimately, the word expresses the relationship of favor: to be chosen means to enjoy the love and protection of the Lord, who brings His chosen ones out in joy (Psalms 105:43). It is a status of privilege and responsibility before God.
H0972.origine: The root means "to choose, to sort." The word builds an image of selection: just as one sorts and selects the best elements, God "chooses" the people and individuals who please Him. This idea of voluntary selection by God is at the heart of the biblical concept of election.
H0972.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Psalms and Isaiah. It always denotes the result of a divine choice: the chosen individuals (David, Moses) receive a special mission and a covenant; the chosen people enjoy divine protection and promise. The context is almost exclusively that of the relationship between God and Israel, marked by unmerited favor and corresponding responsibility. Election is never a right, but an act of grace.
H0972.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that salvation is not a personal conquest, but a choice of God. To be chosen means to be loved freely, called to a covenant, and entrusted with a mission: it is both a comfort and a call to faithfulness. For the believer, discovering that he is chosen places him before the responsibility of living in response to this free love.

sens: To feel a deep repulsion or aversion towards someone or something
To feel impatience mixed with contempt
H0973A.detail:
1. To have disgust means to experience a strong repulsion, an intimate rejection towards someone or something. It is a feeling that raises the soul to disgust and aversion. In Zechariah 11:8, the prophet speaks of the three shepherds whom his soul had in disgust: he deeply rejected them, there was a rupture of covenant and love between them.
2. The word can also express impatience mixed with contempt, a feeling of annoyance that goes beyond simple displeasure. It is the soul turning away with repulsion, like someone who can no longer bear the presence or existence of another.
H0973A.origine: The verb בחל (ba'hal) expresses a movement of the soul that withdraws, that turns away with repulsion. The root evokes the idea of weariness and rupture: the soul (nephesh) can no longer bear it, it rejects. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, painting a feeling of particular intensity, stronger than a simple ordinary aversion.
H0973A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 11:8. The context is that of a broken covenant between the prophet-shepherd and the people: he and they mutually have disgust for each other. This feeling expresses the extremity of separation and mutual rejection, after the relationship of trust has disappeared.
H0973A.portee: This word reminds us that mutual rejection and disgust are the fruits of a broken covenant. It shows how the absence of God's presence and love in a human relationship can create deep repulsion between hearts. It is a warning about the cost of unfaithfulness: not only the rupture, but the disgust that follows.

sens: To examine something or someone carefully to verify its quality or nature
To subject to a difficult trial to test resistance or sincerity
To go through a trial; to undergo a test
To discern, perceive, grasp through the senses or intelligence
H0974.detail:
1. To test is first to examine, scrutinize carefully: just as one verifies gold by heating it in the furnace to see if it holds, one tests someone by putting them in a situation that reveals who they really are (Proverbs 17:3).
2. It is also to subject to a trial: God tests us as silver passes through the crucible, exposing us to difficulty to purify our heart and faith (Psalms 66:10).
3. To test is also what one undergoes when going through a trial; it is to pass through the test, to be put to the test (Genesis 42:15).
4. By extension, it is to discern, to perceive finely: the ear discerns words as the palate savors food, through a kind of sensitive judgment (Job 12:11).
H0974.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּחַן comes from a root that evokes the idea of testing and verifying. The word is linked to the image of metalworking: gold and silver must be heated to be purified and verified. This root thus expresses the action of putting to the test to reveal the true nature of something.
H0974.emploi: The verb is used 28 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Psalms, Job, and Jeremiah. It describes how God tests the hearts and reins of humans (Psalms 7:10, Jeremiah 12:3), how He tests us as fire tests metals (Psalms 66:10, Proverbs 17:3). It can also denote a practical test: Joseph tests his brothers by putting them to the test (Genesis 42:15). In Job, we also see that the ear tests words as the palate tests food (Job 12:11).
H0974.portee: This word reminds Christians that God truly knows our hearts, not out of curiosity but out of love: He tests us to purify and strengthen us, not to condemn us. The trials of life are not random, but opportunities where God helps us become more authentic in our faith.

sens: tall structure built for observation
place of surveillance and defense
H0975.detail:
1. A watchtower is a building constructed at a height to allow for distant viewing and to observe the approach of enemies or dangers. It is a defensive structure typical of fortified cities in biblical times. In Isaiah 32:14, the watchtower of an abandoned city gradually becomes a refuge for wild animals — a sign of complete destruction and desolation.
2. Figuratively, a watchtower represents a strategic observation post, a place from which one watches and protects oneself. It is a symbol of vigilance and security for those who build and defend it.
H0975.origine: The Hebrew word בַּחַן (bahan) or בַּחַן (bachan) comes from a root that evokes the act of scrutinizing, examining, or watching from a high position. It specifically designates the tower or structure serving as an observation post. This type of construction was common in the ancient Near East, both for monitoring roads and borders and for protection during sieges.
H0975.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 32:14. It describes the future state of a ruined city where the palaces and watchtowers, once symbols of power and vigilance, will no longer serve any defense. Wild donkeys and flocks will graze there in desolation, as if nature reclaims the place. This context of universal ruin emphasizes how the tower, which embodied human strength and security, becomes useless when God's judgment falls.
H0975.portee: The watchtower reminds us that all human power and security, no matter how solidly built, are fragile in the face of God's judgment. It invites the reader not to place their trust in earthly fortifications and defenses, but in the protection that only God can provide.

sens: That has been subjected to a trial, a test
That has proven itself, shown to be solid and trustworthy
That has endured a difficulty or suffering and triumphed over it
H0976.detail:
1. The word describes something or someone that has gone through a trial, a test intended to verify its quality or solidity. It conveys the idea of metal being tempered in fire to strengthen it, or a building being subjected to shocks to verify its durability. In Isaiah 28:16, the "tested" stone is one that has been examined and recognized as capable of bearing weight without collapsing: it is reliable.
2. More broadly, the word characterizes what or who has faced trials and emerged intact, even strengthened. A person tested by life is someone who has gone through difficulties and gained wisdom and firmness of character from them. They are worthy of trust.
3. The term can also emphasize the idea of suffering endured and transformed. One who is "tested" in the deep sense has not only passed a trial but has been changed: purified, strengthened, or made more attentive to others who suffer.
H0976.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to put to the test," "to test," or "to try." It is found in contexts where the quality of something is verified by fire, heat, or difficulty — like testing metal in a crucible to see what alloy it is. This root evokes the concrete image of forging and testing: one does not truly know what one has until it is subjected to a trial.
H0976.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible at this point in the Segond translation. It is a relatively rare word, but it carries a strong meaning in this context where the prophet Isaiah speaks of the foundation laid by God in Zion. The "tested" stone is the one that God himself has chosen and tested: it has proven itself, it is capable of supporting those who lean on it. This foundation never disappoints.
H0976.portee: For the believer, this image of the tested stone speaks of deep assurance. God does not lay his foundation lightly: the faith he invites to build is founded on something solid, tested, that has withstood every trial. By resting on this foundation, the Christian does not need to fear collapsing, even on the day of judgment. This word invites one to place their trust not in what is fragile or without foundation, but in what has been tested by God himself.

sens: Deliberately select a person or thing from others
Prefer something as better or more suitable
Decide that someone belongs to a specific function or role
Be the object of such selection or preference
H0977.detail:
1. Deliberately selecting a person or thing from others: this is the act of taking a side for one over the others. In Genesis 6:2, the sons of God "chose" daughters of men to be their wives; this is a concrete choice among several possibilities. At the human level, it denotes any act of preference and decision.
2. Preferring something as better or more suitable: the word expresses that what is chosen is deemed superior. In Proverbs 22:1, "a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches" — this is judging that reputation outweighs wealth.
3. Deciding that someone belongs to a function or role: this is choosing someone for a charge or service. In 1 Samuel 16:8, Samuel seeks among the sons of Jesse the one whom the Lord has "chosen" to be king; it is about designating someone for a role.
4. Being the object of such selection: the word can also express the passive side, that which is chosen. Israel was "chosen" by the Lord (Deuteronomy 7:6) — this people was selected for a special covenant and mission.
H0977.origine: The verb "choose" comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to examine, test, and then select." It is related to the idea of discernment: one chooses after having examined. The word appears in several forms — one can undergo a choice ("be chosen"), or make one ("choose"). This root is also used to express trial or testing: choosing implies knowing and appreciating what one selects.
H0977.emploi: The verb "choose" is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible (about 163 occurrences). It appears mostly in Deuteronomy, where God "chooses" a place to set His sanctuary, or a people to make His treasure. In 1 Samuel 16, Samuel is sent to choose a king from the sons of Jesse: to choose means then to designate someone for a charge. At decisive moments, God invites the people to "choose" — Joshua 24:15: "Choose this day whom you will serve." The word also encompasses ordinary choices (Genesis 13:11, Lot "chose" the fertile region of the Jordan) and expresses the idea that every important choice commits the one who makes it. The context can give the verb a nuance of divine election: it is not just to choose, but to be elected, marked by God.
H0977.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp two major truths. First, that choosing is a serious action: our preferences and decisions engage and define us. Second, that divine election in the Bible does not erase human responsibility — the Lord "chooses" Israel, but Israel must also "choose" to serve. This verb invites the believer to examine their own choices in light of God's will.

sens: Inhabitant or descendant of Bahurim
H0978.detail: The term designates a person from the city of Bahurim or who is a descendant of it. In 1 Chronicles 11:33, Azmaveth is identified as "of Bacharum," indicating his place of origin or his belonging to this family or geographical group. It is a common way in the Bible to designate people by their provenance.
H0978.origine: The word comes from Bahurim (בַּחוּרִים), the name of a city in Israel. The name Bahurim means "choice young men" or "young people." The added suffix creates a demonym — a word that identifies someone as a resident or native of a given place, according to a common practice in Hebrew.
H0978.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:33. It is found in the list of the mighty warriors of King David. Azmaveth, identified as Bacharum, was one of the thirty elite valiant men of the king. This unique mention shows the use of the term to establish the identity and origin of a character in the military and administrative context of the royal era.

sens: Period of human life from childhood to adulthood
Strength, vigor, and abilities of young age
State of inexperience and naivety characteristic of this age
Time when one enjoys pleasures and joys without restraint
H0979.detail:
1. Youth is the period of life that begins after childhood and extends to adulthood: it is the time when one is building oneself, when one is still growing. Joshua served Moses "from his youth" (Numbers 11:28), which means that this bond began when he was a young man.
2. This word also evokes the physical strength and natural energy of this age. Unlike old age, which weakens, youth is the time when the body is vigorous and capable of great things.
3. Youth is also marked by inexperience and a certain innocence: it is the age when one does not yet know everything about life and where one can make mistakes. This explains why youth can be carefree or naive.
4. In the passages of Ecclesiastes (12:1), youth is presented as the time of pleasures, joys, and desires of life: it is the time when "you walk according to the desires of your eyes" and where your heart rejoices freely, before old age arrives.
H0979.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of growing, blooming, and flourishing. Youth is therefore naturally associated with vitality and the expansion of life. In Hebrew, there are words from the same family that retain this notion of freshness and development. This root paints the image of a period when everything is growing, when life is in full bloom.
H0979.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always with the meaning of the young period of life. In Numbers 11:28, it designates the time of Joshua's service to Moses, marking his attachment since his young years. Ecclesiastes uses it twice (12:1 and 12:3) to exhort the young man to rejoice and enjoy life, but also to remind him of his duty to God: one must remember one's Creator during youth, before old age brings the days of trouble. The word thus oscillates between the idea of happy vitality and that of moral responsibility.
H0979.portee: Youth in the Bible is not only the age of strength and pleasure: it is also a responsibility before God. Ecclesiastes reminds us that enjoying life with a joyful heart is good and permitted, but never without forgetting that God will judge us on what we have made of it. It is a call to youth to live fully, but with fear of the Lord and faithfulness.

sens: Location of the tribe of Benjamin, between Jerusalem and the Jordan
H0980.detail: Bachurim is a small town located in the tribe of Benjamin, on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho, towards the Jordan. It appears in the accounts of the troubles that shook the kingdom of David: it is from there that Shimei comes out to curse David in flight (2 Samuel 16:5), and it is also where the messengers of Absalom take refuge, pursued by Ahimaaz and Jonathan (2 Samuel 17:18). The name literally means "village of young men," perhaps suggesting a place populated by young warriors or a colony founded by youth. The biblical references clearly situate it on the path that David takes during his flight from Absalom's revolt, and it remains associated with the memory of Shimei, the Benjamite who curses the king.
H0980.origine: The name Bachurim comes from the Hebrew bachurim (בַּחוּרִים), the plural of bachur (young men), a common term in the Old Testament to designate young warriors or young men of fighting age. It is a Benjaminite city, located east of Jerusalem.
H0980.emploi: Bachurim appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the books of Samuel and Kings, and in specific historical contexts related to the troubles of David's reign. It first appears in the account of David's flight (2 Samuel 16:5, 17:18), where it appears as an important waypoint. It is also mentioned during David's return after Absalom's defeat (2 Samuel 19:16) and finally in David's last counsel to Solomon, where Shimei of Bachurim is cited as a man whom Solomon must watch (1 Kings 2:8). Bachurim is primarily a geographical landmark and a witness to the dramatic events of David's reign.

sens: To utter words without thinking, thoughtlessly
To speak hastily or carelessly, without weighing one's words
To speak with anger or irritation
To utter thoughtless words that engage responsibility
H0981.detail:
1. To speak without thinking, thoughtlessly: this is to let words come out of the mouth without first measuring the consequences. In Leviticus 5:4, it refers to someone who "speaks lightly" and swears to do harm or good, without first considering the seriousness of their oath; they later discover its implications and become guilty.
2. To speak hastily or carelessly: this is a hasty word, which ignores wisdom and prudence. Proverbs 12:18 contrasts the one "who speaks lightly" — whose words "wound like a sword" — with the tongue of the wise that "brings healing."
3. To speak under the influence of irritation: in Psalms 106:33, Moses "spoke lightly" when "they provoked his spirit," showing that this speech arises from emotional agitation rather than reflection.
4. To utter words that engage responsibility: light words are not without consequence; they create guilt and a duty before God, as shown in the context of the law of oaths in Leviticus.
H0981.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּטָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of a word that escapes, that is not held back. The image is that of a light word, without weight, that comes out hastily without control. This root is conceptually close to other Hebrew words expressing lightness or thoughtlessness.
H0981.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Leviticus 5:4, it describes the oath pronounced "lightly" in the law concerning guilt and restitution. In Psalms 106:33, it reports how Moses spoke lightly in a moment of irritation, which cost him entry into the Promised Land. In Proverbs 12:18, it illustrates the contrast between the light word that wounds and the wise tongue that heals, highlighting the moral and spiritual impact of words. The context always shows that speaking lightly has serious consequences.
H0981.portee: This word teaches the believer the gravity of words and the necessity of self-control. Light words — born of impatience, anger, or carelessness — are never without weight; they engage our responsibility before God and can hurt those who listen to us. It is a call to wisdom: to think before speaking, especially in moments of intense emotion, so that our words bring healing rather than harm.

sens: To place one's assurance in someone or something, to believe that they will protect and help us
To have confidence, to be sure not to be disappointed or abandoned
To be safe, without fear, at peace in one's soul
To rely on someone or something instead of counting on oneself
H0982.detail:
1. To trust means to hand over one's heart and worries to someone else, firmly believing that they will know how to save or protect us. Psalm 115:11 expresses this well: "You who fear the Lord, trust in the Lord! He is their help and their shield" — meaning: surrender your fear into His hands.
2. To have confidence also means to be internally sure that one will not be deceived, that one can count on the word or strength of the one in whom they trust. In Psalm 41:10, the psalmist speaks of the traitor: "Even my close friend, whom I trusted, who shared my bread" — to have his trust was for David the certainty of true friendship.
3. To be safe or without fear: the word also evokes the tranquil peace that comes when one ceases to fear. Isaiah 26:3: "You will keep in perfect peace those whose minds are steadfast, because they trust in you" — trust removes anxiety and gives profound peace.
4. To rely on someone means to stop trying to control everything by one's own strength. Proverbs 3:5 encourages us: "Trust in the Lord with all your heart" — this is to acknowledge that we need Him, that we cannot do everything alone.
H0982.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of throwing oneself into someone's arms, of taking refuge. In Hebrew, it is linked to the image of rest and security: someone who trusts surrenders, they cease to defend themselves alone. The same root also gives the word for "security" and "trust" — three nuances of the same inner gesture.
H0982.emploi: This verb is very common in the Hebrew Bible (117 times), especially in the Psalms and Proverbs. The Psalms use it to speak of trust in God in the face of danger or uncertainty. Proverbs uses it to urge the wise to trust in God rather than in their own strength. Among the kings of Israel, like Hezekiah in 2 Kings 18, the verb shows how one had to choose between trusting in God or in human alliances. Deuteronomy warns: do not trust in walls or your riches; Jeremiah accuses Israel of trusting in false hopes (Jeremiah 7:4). The biblical usage nuances the word: to trust in God alone is true wisdom, while trusting in men, wealth, or our own strength is vanity.
H0982.portee: For the believer, this word calls for a surrender of trust in God. It invites us to let go of our fears and efforts to control, and to rest on divine faithfulness. It is an invitation to inner peace — not an absence of wisdom or vigilance, but a deep conviction that God will not abandon us. The word summarizes an entire Christian posture: to count less on oneself, and more on Him.

sens: The state of one who has nothing to fear, who is safe from danger
Tranquil confidence in present or future well-being
Absence of fear in the face of a possible threat
H0983.detail:
1. Security is primarily the state of one who lives without immediate fear of danger. In Genesis 34:25, the city believed it was "secure" at the very moment when Simeon and Levi struck it: it is a refuge, an impression of peace that can be fragile. In Deuteronomy 33:28, Israel is "secure in its dwelling," meaning established in a protected place where it can breathe.
2. The word also denotes a tranquil confidence, a rest of the mind in the face of what could disturb. In Proverbs 3:29, the neighbor dwells "securely" when he suspects nothing of the evil that is being plotted against him. Job 24:23 speaks of giving "security and confidence": it is to place someone in a calm state of mind.
3. Finally, security can mean the lasting absence of threat, an established protection. Ezekiel 34:27 promises that the peoples will be "secure in their land" when God has broken their bonds: it is a complete deliverance, a safe environment.
H0983.origine: The Hebrew word bétach comes from a root that evokes the idea of trust and refuge. It is related to the verb "to trust" and the noun "trust." In the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, it often corresponds to the Greek "asphaleia" (safety) or "pepoithesis" (confidence). The underlying image is that of someone who rests, who can finally relax their muscles because they have nothing to dread.
H0983.emploi: The word bétach appears 41 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom literature (Proverbs, Job, Psalms) and prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It first describes the peace of a city or people without an enemy: Israel secure in its dwelling (Deuteronomy 33:28), a city that believes it is secure (Genesis 34:25). It also expresses personal confidence: that of the righteous who rests in peace (Psalms 4:9), that which a friend inspires when one suspects nothing wrong (Proverbs 3:29). Finally, it becomes a messianic promise: the peace that God establishes for His people (Jeremiah 23:6, Ezekiel 34:27). Security can be deceptive (a city naive enough to let down its guard) or authentic (the one that only God can give).
H0983.portee: This word shows that true peace is not the absence of vigilance, but a deep rest in trust. For the Christian, it reminds us that security comes from God alone and not from our own strength: that is why the prophets promise a security that no enemy can disturb. It also invites us to examine what our own tranquility rests upon: is it naivety or trust in God?

sens: city of the kingdom of Zobah during the reign of King Hadadezer
H0984.detail: Bethach is a city that was part of the kingdom of Zobah under the reign of Hadadezer, an Aramean king contemporary with David. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 8:8, as one of the places from which David took and seized bronze during his victory over Hadadezer.
H0984.origine: The name Bethach literally means "house of security" in Hebrew ("beth" = house, "tach" = security), although this original meaning is likely a play on words or a popular etymology. It is an Aramean city located in northern Syria, in the historical region of the Levant.
H0984.emploi: Bethach appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 8:8. It is cited among the cities conquered by King David during his military campaign against Hadadezer, king of Zobah. David took a large amount of bronze from there, which he brought back to Jerusalem. This mention illustrates the extent of David's conquests and the wealth he amassed to build the temple.

sens: Attitude of one who relies entirely on someone or something
Inner tranquility based on the certainty of being protected or helped
Fearless surrender to the goodness and power of God
H0985.detail:
1. Trust is the attitude of the heart that relies entirely on someone — here on the Lord — without doubt or anxiety. In Isaiah 30:15, it appears alongside tranquility and rest, as the true strength of the people of Israel in the face of threats.

2. It is an inner tranquility, a serenity of heart, that arises from the certainty that God protects us and will intervene to save us. When the prophet speaks of "calm and trust," he describes a state of peace that contrasts with fear and agitation.

3. At a deeper level, it is the complete surrender of the believer to divine goodness and power. It is not a vague or naive trust, but a conscious choice: to reject futile human efforts and to fully entrust oneself to God.
H0985.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root בטח (bataḥ), which means in its primary sense "to stretch out, to relax" — the image of the body that relaxes because it is safe. This root expresses the idea of throwing oneself into someone's arms with abandon, entrusting everything that concerns us. The word bitchah is a form of the noun that is also found at the root of the verb "to trust" in many psalms.
H0985.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 30:15. At this crucial moment in the prophetic message, the Lord contrasts two paths: that of the people who flee to Egypt and rely on horses (previous verses), and the one that God proposes — to wait in peace and trust. This context shows that trust is presented as the antidote to panic and self-deliverance. It is a word addressed to a people in political danger, to teach them that true salvation comes from surrendering to God, not from diplomatic or military alliances.
H0985.portee: For the Christian today, this word teaches that trust in God is not an escape into illusion, but an authentic strength. Isaiah 30:15 invites the believer in danger to renounce their own anxious efforts and to discover that the rest and tranquility of heart — nourished by trust — are the true source of spiritual strength and salvation.

sens: Support, backing on which one firmly relies
State of one who trusts someone or something without fear
Hope, assurance of a favorable outcome
H0986.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the concrete support on which one relies: when the king of Assyria challenges King Hezekiah, he provokes him by asking, "On what trust do you rely?" (Isaiah 36:4), that is, on what support, what reliable ally. It is the image of a person leaning against someone or something stable.
2. By extension, it is the inner state of a person who trusts someone without doubting or fearing — a tranquility of heart based on the certainty that the trusted person will not abandon you.
3. It is also hope, the assurance that something good will happen: "For all who live there is hope" (Ecclesiastes 9:4), a positive glimmer of the future even in difficulty.
H0986.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means to lean, to rest upon. It evokes the physical image of someone leaning on an object or person to support themselves with all their weight — hence the idea of depending entirely, of trusting. Biblical trust is never a light matter, but a solid support, the resting of one's entire being on something firm.
H0986.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In the two parallel passages of 2 Kings 18:19 and Isaiah 36:4, it refers to political or military trust — that which a king places in his allies or forces. It is a concrete, contestable, fragile trust. In Ecclesiastes 9:4, the meaning shifts toward existential hope: even one who lives in uncertainty has a reason to hope, because life itself is a good. The word changes register according to its object: trust in human powers (risky) or trust in life and the future (deeper).
H0986.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that trust is a positioning of the heart: one does not trust passively, one leans on someone. The Bible confronts us with these questions: on what or whom do I truly lean? On uncertain human powers, or on God who never fails? To trust in God is to transfer the support of one's soul from perishable realities to the one who alone is worthy of this total rest.

sens: State of one who is safe from danger, peril
Tranquil assurance, feeling of trust without real foundation
H0987.detail:
1. Security is the absence of danger, the feeling of being protected and sheltered. In Job 12:6, it refers to the rest that robbers find under their tent — a physical safety, a refuge where they feel out of reach.
2. But this verse reveals an important nuance: it is also a false trust, a deceptive security. The text shows violent men "who offend God" enjoying an apparent tranquility, as if they believed themselves invulnerable. It is an assurance without true foundation, a security that real danger threatens without their knowledge.
H0987.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be confident" or "to rely on." It expresses the idea of a person who fears nothing, who believes they are safe — whether they are right or wrong. The same root produces words for "trust" and "assurance": it describes the psychological state of one who feels secure.
H0987.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 12:6. In this unique passage, Job contemplates the injustice of the world: the tents of robbers enjoy peace, the provocateurs live in security, as if God were asleep. It is a cry of revolt against deceptive appearances: those who violate justice seem to live without worry, and Job is scandalized by it. This verse thus raises the question of the real foundation of security: is it true when it rests on injustice?
H0987.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on true security. It does not come from strength, wealth, or the temporary absence of danger, but from a covenant with God. The security of the wicked, even if it seems solid, is illusory and precarious. In contrast, trust in God offers lasting safety, based not on circumstances, but on divine faithfulness.

sens: To bend down, to incline downward
To lose strength, capacity for action
To cease, to stop functioning
H0988.detail:
1. To bend means to fold something or someone downward, like bending one's back. It is the physical movement of something that inclines: a branch that bends under weight, a person who leans.
2. Figuratively, the word describes the gradual loss of strength and activity. As one ages, the body bends and weakens: one loses the ability to stand upright, to act as before. This idea of decline is expressed in Ecclesiastes 12:5.
3. To bend can also simply mean to cease, to stop: a function that is no longer exercised, an action that comes to an end. Strong men bend, meaning they weaken and cease to function at full power.
H0988.origine: The Hebrew verb בָּטַל (batàl) belongs to a family of words that revolve around the idea of bending, yielding, weakening. The word first denotes the physical movement of the body that inclines, then by extension, wear, weakness, and cessation of vigor. In Aramaic, the related word בְּטֵל (betèl) carries the same meaning: to cease, to stop.
H0988.emploi: The verb appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in this passage from the book of Ecclesiastes. The author describes the signs of old age: the text states that "strong men bend," a poetic image of the decline of strength. It is not merely a simple inclination of the body, but the description of the moment when vigor abandons a man and he can no longer act with his former power. This is why the translation "bend" captures both the physical image and the underlying idea of weakening and end.
H0988.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible acknowledges the wear of time and the natural decline of the human body. It does not hide this reality: aging is a fact that the wise observe and accept. For the believer, this passage invites us to reflect on what truly matters beyond physical strength — wisdom, faith, and relationship with God remain when the body weakens. It is also an exhortation to live wisely and justly from youth.

sens: To stop an ongoing action, to suspend work or activity
To cause something to interrupt, to impose a stop
To leave an interruption, a pause in continuity
H0989.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of an activity that stops or comes to an end: to stop doing something, to suspend an occupation. In Ezra 4:24, the word describes how the work of the house of God in Jerusalem "stopped" — the work simply ceased, as if the productive machine had frozen. It is the natural transition from movement to stillness.
2. The second meaning is more active: to order or cause something to cease, to impose a stop by force. In Ezra 4:21-23, the king orders to "make cease" the work of the Jews, and this order is executed: the adversaries will "make cease their work by violence and force." The word then carries the idea of a forced, deliberate interruption.
3. The third meaning concerns the absence of continuity, the presence of a break or interruption in a process. In Ezra 6:8, the king declares that the money will be paid "so that there is no interruption" — that is, so that the work does not stop, does not experience these frustrating breaks. Here, the word names the interruption itself rather than the action of ceasing.
H0989.origine: The Aramaic verb בְּטֵל comes from a root that evokes the idea of becoming empty, null, or ineffective. The corresponding Hebrew root (בטל) carries the same meaning: to render something inactive, without force, without result. The word denotes the functional annihilation of an action — not its physical destruction, but its inability to continue or produce.
H0989.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears 5 times in the Bible, all in the book of Ezra, which recounts the return of the Jews from exile and the reconstruction of the Temple. The usages focus on a critical moment: when the adversaries of the Jews obtain from the king an order prohibiting the reconstruction of the Temple (Ezra 4). The verb first designates the king's order to "make cease" the work (4:21), then its violent execution (4:23), and finally the ensuing stop (4:24). Later, when King Darius allows the resumption, the same word appears to describe how God prevents the work from experiencing "interruption" (5:5 and 6:8). The word always carries the idea of a suspension of work, whether voluntary or imposed.
H0989.portee: This word reminds the reader how external obstacles — even powerful and official ones — can paralyze a work, but also how God ensures that His project is realized despite interruptions. The work on the Temple ceases, but is not annulled: God ensures its resumption. For the Christian, this is an assurance that temporary obstacles do not frustrate the fulfillment of God's will, provided one perseveres in faith.

sens: The area of the body between the chest and the hips
The physical seat of hunger and appetite
The seat of thoughts and intimate feelings
The womb, the maternal belly
The interior of a place or creature (figurative)
H0990G.detail:
1. The belly is primarily the anatomical belly, the part of the body between the chest and the hips. It is in this sense that Ehud thrusts his sword into the belly of the king (Judges 3:21).
2. The belly is the seat of hunger and appetite: it is through the belly that one experiences hunger and tastes satiety. Thus, eating the fruit of one's mouth "satisfies the belly" (Proverbs 18:20).
3. The belly also symbolizes the place of secret thoughts and desires: it is where intentions and hidden emotions germinate. Job says that his insides boil with a word he must announce (Job 32:19).
4. The belly can refer to the womb, the maternal breast from which the child is born, in a woman.
5. By extension, the belly denotes the deep interior of something: Jonah speaks of the belly of the great fish (Jonah 2:3), figuratively representing the underground abode.
H0990G.origine: The Hebrew word beten comes from a root that designates what is hollow, enveloping, containing. The belly is literally what encloses, what carries. In Hebrew, the family of this word includes other words expressing interiority and what fills. The belly is thought of as the quintessential cavity of the human body.
H0990G.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible. It appears mainly in the Poems and Wisdom (Job, Proverbs, Psalms). In historical narratives (Judges), it refers to the anatomical belly as a mortal seat (the sword that pierces Eglon). In Wisdom, it designates the seat of appetites (hunger, greed) and hidden feelings. In poetry (Job, Psalms), it symbolizes the deep, emotional, or spiritual interior. Ezekiel uses the belly figuratively when speaking of the absorption of the written scroll, and Jonah evokes the belly of the fish as a symbol of the underground abode.
H0990G.portee: Understanding that the belly is for the Bible much more than just a part of the body: it is the image of our desires, our inner hunger, the deepest part of ourselves. This reminds the reader that our appetites, our hidden thoughts, our true intentions find their source not in our reason alone, but in our guts. It is an invitation to examine what truly moves us, to be honest with ourselves about what drives us.

sens: The organ of the body that contains the intestines, the seat of digestion
The womb, the uterus of the mother before birth
The state of pregnancy, the condition of the fetus before birth
Metaphorically, the seat of emotions and thoughts
Metaphorically, the heart or the intimate intention
H0990H.detail:
1. The belly is primarily the abdomen, the part of the body where the viscera are located: this is why one can speak of the belly as the seat of hunger (Deuteronomy 28:4 mentions the fruit of the belly in parallel with crops and herds), or as the center of bodily sensations and desires.
2. The belly is also and above all the maternal womb, the maternal breast where the child is formed before birth. When Scripture says that Samson was consecrated "from his mother's belly" (Judges 16:17), it refers to the moment of his conception, even before he was born.
3. Pregnancy itself can be called belly: the children growing in the mother's belly, before coming into the world, are the "fruit of the belly" (Psalms 127:3). Isaiah says to Jacob: "from your birth," where the Hebrew literally says "from your belly."
4. Because of this intimate link between the mother and the child in the belly, the word belly becomes an image of deep intention or heart: what germinates in the belly is what is most secret, most true.
5. The belly can finally metaphorically designate the heart or the hidden seat of intentions (Job 15:35 speaks of the belly that gives birth to wickedness).
6. In the biblical imagery of the world of the dead, the belly of Sheol represents the abyss that engulfs the dead.
H0990H.origine: The Hebrew word for belly (betèn) refers to the living body as the seat of vital energy, growth, and formation. Its fundamental image is that of the generative cavity: the belly of the woman where life is formed, but also the belly of every creature as the center of physical being. It is a fundamental word in Hebrew physiology, often designating what is deepest, most intimate in the body and the person.
H0990H.emploi: The word belly appears 46 times in the Old Testament, especially in the poetic books (Psalms, Job) and in prophetic speeches. It regularly returns to speak of the fertility or sterility of a woman's belly (Genesis 25:23 shows two children in the same belly, Jacob and Esau): it is a sign of divine blessing to have children from the belly, and a curse to be deprived of them. Scripture also uses it to evoke the moment of conception and birth: Jeremiah, Samson, John the Baptist are all consecrated "from the belly" or "before birth." By extension, the belly becomes an image of the secret, the intimate, what springs from the deepest part of oneself (thoughts, malicious intentions spring from the belly).
H0990H.portee: The word belly reminds us that God knows us and forms us even before our birth, intimately, like a child in its mother's womb. It is a call to see our life as a gift formed by the hand of God from the beginning, and to understand that what springs from the depths of us — our intentions, our thoughts, our words — reveals our true nature. It invites us to ask God to purify our heart and our intentions, from the very source.

sens: Rounded protuberance on a surface
Belly or abdomen of the body
Uterine cavity, womb
Seat of emotions and thoughts
H0990I.detail:
1. The word first designates a rounded protuberance, a swelling: in 1 Kings 7:20, it refers to the decorative bulge of a bronze column, a kind of ornamental bump placed between the network of the base and the capital.
2. By extension, it designates the belly, the abdomen — the part of the body that rounds and swells. It is the concrete seat of hunger and satiety.
3. It can also mean the womb, the maternal belly from which life emerges — the image of the breast and gestation.
4. In ancient Hebrew thought, the belly is not just a simple organ: it is a seat of emotions, compassion, inner turmoil, and deep thoughts, as seen in other biblical texts where the heart and belly relate together to inner life.
H0990I.origine: The Hebrew word בֶטֶן comes from a root that evokes the idea of swelling, of protuberance. Its primary image is that of a surface that bulges, that stands out in relief. In Hebrew, the belly is often associated with the seat of emotions and vital sensations — not reason (the heart or the head), but the instinctive and emotional life of the body.
H0990I.emploi: This word appears only once in the provided Segond translation, in 1 Kings 7:20, where it describes an architectural element: the bulge of a column in Solomon's temple. But in the Hebrew Old Testament, the word is much more frequent and has several meanings: the belly as a physical organ, the feminine womb, and in several passages it designates the seat of emotions — compassion springs from the belly, fear knots it, joy expands it. This is why ancient translations, like the Vulgate, rendered this word as "viscera" in many cases.
H0990I.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not separate the body from the soul and emotions as an abstract philosophical thought might. It sees the whole person: the belly is not shameful, it is the place where life is tied, where compassion germinates, where terror or joy is born. Understanding that our emotions inhabit our flesh is to recognize that we are embodied beings, not floating spirits.

sens: Lower part of the body, between the chest and the hips
Womb, place of conception and gestation
Seat of deep emotions and thoughts
Depth, interior of a person
Descendants, offspring
H0990J.detail:
1. The belly primarily designates the abdomen, the physical seat of the body. When the Lord threatens an unfaithful woman in Numbers 5:21, He evokes the swelling of her belly as a sign of curse.
2. It is also the womb, the place where life is formed. Psalms 132:11 speaks of a "fruit of your loins," meaning a child directly from the one who bears it.
3. The belly is the seat of feeling, sensation, and inner wisdom. Job 32:18 says, "the spirit presses within me": it is deep within the belly that words boil. Proverbs 18:8 shows how the words of the reporter "descend to the depths of the belly," they engrave there.
4. The belly also represents the interior of a person, their innermost being where they keep words (Proverbs 22:18).
5. By metonymy, the bowels designate descendants: what comes out of the belly, children.
H0990J.origine: The Hebrew word בֶּטֶן comes from a root that means "hollow" or "depressed." It literally designates the cavity of the lower belly. The word is often used in the plural "entrails" in French, which better conveys the Hebrew when speaking of depth, interiority, or feeling. It is a very common word in the Old Testament to express the seat of emotions and thought.
H0990J.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Segond translations. It is mainly found in the Psalms and Proverbs, books of wisdom and prayer. In Numbers 5:21, it is purely physical: the swelling of the belly. In Job 32:18 and Proverbs 18:8, it becomes the place of thought and inner feeling — what "descends" or "presses" in the belly symbolizes a deep, almost unavoidable reality. In Psalms 132:11, it designates descendants, begetting. Psalms 31:10 shows the body in its fragility in the face of distress. The word thus glides from the physical to the emotional and spiritual.
H0990J.portee: This word reminds us that the body is not an empty shell: it is the seat of feeling, desire, and wisdom. When the Bible speaks of the belly, it tells us that our emotions, our deep thoughts, our rooted reactions are realities that matter before God. It is an invitation to examine our "entrails" — what motivates us at the most intimate level.

sens: city of the tribe of Asher in ancient Israel
H0991.detail: Bethen is a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher during the division of Canaan among the Israelites (Joshua 19:25). It is mentioned in the list of cities that marked the boundaries of Asher's territory, alongside Helkath and Acschaph.
H0991.origine: The name Bethen literally means "belly" or "breast" in Hebrew (from the root בטן), but it refers here to a geographical location whose exact name likely reflects the meaning given to this place by its founders or inhabitants.
H0991.emploi: Bethen appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:25, where it is listed among the border cities of Asher's territory. It is part of the administrative description of the territorial boundaries of this tribe after the conquest of Canaan.

sens: edible dry fruit of the pistachio tree
luxurious and prestigious food offered as a gift
H0992.detail:
1. The pistachio is the fruit of the pistachio tree, a nut or seed that can be eaten, whether fresh or dried. It is the ancient equivalent of the dried fruits we know: nutritious, tasty, and easy to transport.
2. In Genesis 43:11, Jacob sends pistachios as part of the gift brought to Egypt: this is not just any food, but a precious commodity, a refined product offered to someone of importance. Pistachios are listed alongside balm, honey, spices, and myrrh—all rare and expensive goods. It is a sign of respect and honor.
H0992.origine: The Hebrew word bottenim specifically refers to this fruit. It likely comes from the Eastern Mediterranean, where the pistachio tree grew and where this fruit had been cultivated since antiquity. The word accurately reflects the botanical and commercial reality of the time.
H0992.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 43:11. Jacob fills his sons with instructions: he sends them to get grain in Egypt, and he asks them to bring a gift to the one who receives them—a gift that includes various goods from the land of Canaan, among which are pistachios. The context shows that this is an act of diplomacy and respect towards Joseph, the governor of Egypt (whom Jacob does not recognize).
H0992.portee: This detail invites the reader to discover how Jacob honors the one who can help him: not out of pride, but with a humble and precious gift, carefully chosen from the products of his land. It is a model of the reverence we are called to show to those in power and authority, without servility but with dignity.

sens: City of Gad, east of the Jordan
H0993.detail: Bethonim is a city located in the territory of Gad, in the region east of the Jordan. It appears in the land distribution to the tribes of Israel during the conquest of Canaan. It is a border locality mentioned between Heshbon and Mahanaim (Joshua 13:26).
H0993.origine: The name Bethonim literally means "pistachio nuts" in Hebrew, suggesting that the region was known for producing this tree. It is a minor locality in ancient Israel, whose name has been preserved in biblical texts.
H0993.emploi: Bethonim is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 13:26. It appears in the context of the land distribution among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of the land, particularly in the portion assigned to the tribe of Gad. It is located east of the Jordan, in a border area between several important cities.

sens: polite phrase to introduce a request or prayer
exclamation to express regret or embarrassment
pleading call addressed to someone in authority
H0994.detail:
1. This word is an interjection, that is, a cry or a set phrase placed before a request to make it more courteous. In Genesis 43:20, Joseph's brothers say "Pardon, my lord" when addressing the Egyptian steward: they want to implore his indulgence before speaking to him. It is like saying "I pray you" or "please."
2. It also expresses embarrassment or fear in speaking to someone. Moses uses it in Exodus 4:10: "Ah, Lord!" he says, before confessing that he is not able to speak. Gideon does the same in Judges 6:13, starting with "Ah, my lord!" to raise a difficulty before the angel of the Lord.
3. It is a form of humble supplication. When Aaron says in Numbers 12:11, "Please, my lord, do not hold this sin against us," he seeks to soften Moses with his pleading tone. Manoah similarly proceeds in Judges 13:8: he begins with "Ah, Lord!" to address a respectful prayer to the God who has just spoken to him.
H0994.origine: This Hebrew word is an interjection, meaning it does not conjugate or decline like other words. It belongs to the class of particles, which are small tools of language used to express feelings or structure discourse. Its origin goes back to the earliest Hebrew; it naturally expresses a heartfelt call or a form of politeness towards a superior.
H0994.emploi: This word appears twelve times in the Hebrew Old Testament, almost exclusively in historical and narrative accounts (Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings). Its three main translations in English reflect three nuances: "Ah" marks an interjection expressing emotion or embarrassment (Exodus 4:10, Judges 6:13, Judges 13:8); "Pardon" or "Please" indicate a formula of politeness or supplication (Genesis 43:20, Numbers 12:11, 1 Kings 3:17). In all cases, the speaker addresses someone more powerful or in authority: a master, a king, an angel, or God Himself. It is always a gesture of deference before presenting a request or confessing a difficulty.
H0994.portee: This word shows us how the believers of the Old Testament approached God and the powerful with respect and humility. It reminds us that presenting a request or admitting a difficulty requires courage, and that the tone with which we speak to God and others is important. It is a lesson in politeness, but also in trust: these men and women dared to speak to God despite their weakness or guilt.

sens: Perceive, discern something through the senses or the mind
Grasp the meaning of a word, a story, a riddle
Know, be aware of something in one's heart or mind
Be attentive to, pay attention to, observe
Possess intelligence, wisdom, discernment
Make understood, teach, instruct
